articles.title: MacBook Pro PROLED XDR Reviews Are In: Is the Touchscreen Worth It?
articles.content: The first reviews of the new 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro models with PROLED XDR displays have been published ahead of the laptops launching on Friday. One of the key new features is a touchscreen. Is it worth it, though? Here's what reviews say. The Verge 's David Pierce said that, in his testing so far, touch input has not been something that "meaningfully changes the laptop experience." He recommends the new MacBook Pro models regardless for the OLED display and other upgrades. Pierce did mention some examples where touch proved useful: That's not to say the touchscreen doesn't come in handy, though. It does more often than I expected. When I'm editing photos, reaching out and spreading my fingers to zoom in on the section I want to see is vastly easier than clicking and dragging with the trackpad. When I'm watching a movie, I can just tap the video rather than wiggling the mouse to find the cursor. My favorite touch use so far has been when I'm showing somebody something on my computer — now we can both swipe between options or tap to make an edit rather than having to crowd around the trackpad. He also pointed out a few limitations: There's no onscreen keyboard that appears when you tap a text box; you don't get the copy / paste / select all pop-up when you tap on words. No radius of tools appears when you tap the Apple Pencil on the screen in Procreate, because, oh wait, the Apple Pencil doesn't work at all. Gizmodo 's Kyle Barr said touch input is beneficial for the iPhone Mirroring feature on the Mac: The touchscreen is occasionally useful. It's not the end-all-be-all. But it sure is handy. If you're one to use the iPhone mirroring feature on MacBook Pro, the touchscreen makes it more intuitive. Instead of having to click on the bottom bar to minimize an app, you can simply swipe up from the bottom of the mirrored iPhone, like normal. Using the touchscreen on the mirrored iPhone isn't as snappy as the real deal. It's obvious though that Apple has been working towards this touchscreen design for a while, as more and more macOS features start to make better sense with the touchscreen in tow. WIRED 's Luke Larsen often forgot about the touchscreen, but he too pointed out a few examples where it proved to be useful in his testing: In the time I've had with the touchscreen MacBook Pro so far, I tried to remind myself of its new powers. But when I'm deep in work, I completely forget the touchscreen. It just has no place in my workflows. That doesn't mean it's not ever useful, though. Sometimes, swiping away a notification with a finger feels intuitive. Or if you're lounging on the couch and use your thumb to scroll through your Instagram feed as you would on an iPad, it works. But those times are few and far between. I'm certainly not going to be poking three fingers up at the screen to swipe between Spaces when I could do that on a trackpad without even lifting my hand. With an OLED display, the new MacBook Pro models deliver more vivid colors and increased contrast ratio compared to the previous models with mini-LED displays. The laptops also achieve up to 2,000 nits of brightness for HDR content. OLED displays do not have a backlight, and individual pixels turn off completely for the color black. Bloomberg 's Chris Welch said the OLED display is "genuinely striking": The new MacBook Pro's dual-layer tandem OLED panel is genuinely striking and can get noticeably brighter than LCD models. Since each pixel is individually controlled and can fully shut off for dark content, this screen provides meaningfully superior contrast compared with the Mini LED models, which were already impressive in their own right. Any concerns I had about display uniformity, which can be an issue with some OLED devices, quickly vanished once I began using the machine. From corner to corner, the 16.3-inch panel is punchy, vibrant and can display an even wider range of colors than before — a win for photographers. Mashable 's Timothy Beck Werth…

articles.title: Tobacco company got smoked by leaving secret recipes on a file share
articles.content: Welcome once again to PWNED, where all of the security victims are self-owned. Today, we celebrate a company that makes a supremely unhealthy product having a supremely unhealthy security posture. Our tale of terrible data management, once again, comes courtesy of professional pen tester and red teamer Dahvid Schloss. Assigned to find flaws in the network of a tobacco company, Schloss stumbled onto some very poorly protected trade secrets. Schloss started by probing the network with tools like Metasploit, a popular open-source pen testing app. Surprisingly, the company’s Trend Micro antivirus did not issue an alert even as he was scanning the network for vulnerabilities. He compared the process to shooting a machine gun and having no one hear it. "I'm running through this environment, and I'm basically just using the loudest toys and tools you can imagine," he told The Register. It seemed as if the client simply didn't care much. "I'm feeling like there's not a whole lot of value that I'm providing here." Schloss then asked his boss what else he could do to make his findings more useful and compelling to the client. "My senior manager turns to me and goes 'Think about what is important to this organization. If it got leaked, how detrimental would it be to their business?'" Schloss said. "I’m thinking it’s a products company. Maybe their recipes." Schloss began searching for network file shares that allowed unauthenticated or anonymous access. After discovering an open share, he scanned it using the network mapping tool Nmap . The scan revealed that ports 139 and 445 were open , indicating that the system was running the Windows SMB file sharing protocol . Despite hosting sensitive IT and HR reco rds, this specific file share had no access restrictions and was completely exposed to every employee in the company. He clicked through the directories and found a folder named “confidential." He found files in there which were named recipe, the product name, the sub product name, and the date. He opened one file and discovered that it had information about how that tobacco product was made, including the weight and volume and what percentage of each chemical it had inside. The file was marked with red letters at the top that said "Confidential" and another set at the bottom that said "Do not share." “I think we found a smoking gun here. This is pretty bad,” Schloss said. He noted that anyone on the network could simply use Windows Explorer to find the file. Schloss downloaded the file, thinking he'd be able to show it to the company to prove that the data could be exfiltrated. But his manager asked him to delete the downloaded file, because it was such sensitive information that he shouldn't retain a copy. This would later harm his ability to show that it had ever existed at all. He then told the security team at the tobacco company what he had found, expecting them to lock down all the recipe files. But when he returned to the site the next morning, he got a big surprise: His contact came by and told him that the recipes he found were not real. He denied the files had ever existed and that there was a security problem at all. "And we're just kind of baffled because we're like, what? What are you talking about? This is clearly a recipe you guys have," Schloss said. "It's in the right department. It's in the right folder structure, it's named the right way. Anybody who saw this would consider this a recipe." He listed the recipe files in his security report, but the security people at the tobacco company vehemently denied that the files were real or that he had seen a real recipe. They continued arguing about it for a year and Schloss could not show them the recipe file he had downloaded because he had been forced to erase it. "The funny thing is, I went back and checked towards the end of the engagement to see if those files are still in that folder. And no, they were gone, they were deleted or moved, or something," he said. "So…

articles.title: Exclusive: Nurx And Journey Clinical Co-Founders Raise $6M For Mental Health Startup Siggy
articles.content: Siggy has raised $6 million in pre-seed funding to build a mental health service that uses AI to collect patients’ histories and track progress between appointments with licensed clinicians, the startup told Crunchbase News exclusively. The company brings together two founders who previously built businesses that help patients get treatment outside a traditional doctor’s office. Jonathan Sabbagh co-founded Journey Clinical , which supports practices offering ketamine-assisted psychotherapy, and Edvard Engesæth co-founded Nurx , which provides birth control and other healthcare services online. Village Global led the financing for New York-based Siggy. Notably, several investors in the round previously backed one or both founders. They include Albert Wenger of Union Square Ventures , Mercury co-founder Immad Akhund , and Cityblock Health co-founder Toyin Ajayi , through Coalition Operators . Other participants include PsyMed Ventures , Mystic Ventures and Gokul Rajaram . Jonathan Sabbagh and Edvard Engesæth, co-founders of Siggy. (Courtesy photo) The founders said they began building Siggy in late 2025. The round, which they plan to use to hire more clinicians and engineers, develop the software and work on regulatory requirements, is the first outside funding for the company. The startup recently began accepting paying patients ahead of its public launch, and the founders said they next plan to test the service with paying patients before expanding further. Between appointments Sabbagh, Siggy’s CEO, told Crunchbase News in an interview that the company is addressing a problem he encountered in mental healthcare. Therapists and the clinicians prescribing their patients’ medication often work separately. Patients may see a therapist weekly but have only a brief appointment every few months with their prescriber. This leaves little time or opportunity to discuss changes in symptoms or medication side effects. To address that problem, Siggy uses AI conversations and daily check-ins to gather information clinicians can review between visits. “AI helps maintain the conversation and organize what patients share, so clinicians have a richer picture of the person that they’re treating,” said Engesæth, the startup’s COO, in an interview. Patients begin by answering questions about their history through a free AI conversation. They then meet a licensed clinician by video, who reviews that information. The clinician then makes a diagnosis and prescribes medication if appropriate. Patients can talk with Siggy’s AI between appointments and can also check in each day to report their sleep, mood, medication and how they feel physically. The company combines those answers with data from connected wearable devices to produce a daily “Siggy Score” out of 100. The score is visible to both the patient and clinician. Patients can opt to connect wearables such as Whoop , Oura or Apple Watch, adding sleep, activity, heart rate and heart rate variability data to the daily check-ins that underpin the Siggy Score. The company aims to use those patterns to flag difficult stretches earlier, including when patients report feeling fine despite worsening sleep or other physical changes. If the score changes, the software flags it for a clinician to review. Patients also receive weekly check-ins during their first eight weeks of treatment, according to the company. Clinicians decide whether to continue treatment or adjust medication, and also handle all medical questions. When appropriate, they can help patients taper off gradually. Siggy does not prescribe controlled substances and is not a crisis service, the founders said. One important note: Patients can continue seeing their existing therapists while using Siggy, Sabbagh said. A planned feature would let patients share information with other providers and involve loved ones in their care. articles.title: The Wizard of Open Weights: Chris Alexiuk Makes AI Easy With Open Models
articles.content: Chris Alexiuk has a simple rule about open source AI: If you believe in it, be loud about it. “We should be shouting about this technology from the rooftops,” said Alexiuk, a Toronto-based senior product research engineer in deep learning at NVIDIA who specializes in making open large language models (LLMs) practical for working developers. Alexiuk’s preferred “rooftop” is YouTube , where he’s built a following teaching curious thousands how to build, fine-tune, evaluate and ship production LLM applications and agents. “I think the people who will most help us understand how to build and apply AI likely haven’t even heard of it yet,” he said. “Trying to get knowledge and information out to as many people as humanly possible is what continues to drive me.” Bringing NVIDIA Nemotron to Developers Everywhere Having spent years teaching developers to build with open models, Alexiuk has concluded that transparency isn’t a feature of good AI; it’s the precondition for it. “Fully open source AI is necessary for the democratization of intelligence,” he said. “You should have access to the weights, the data that went into it, the training recipes, everything.” That’s why, on his LinkedIn profile, Alexiuk styles himself “No. 1 Nemotron Fan,” referring to the NVIDIA Nemotron family of open source, multimodal models built for long-running, self-evolving and specialized AI agents. “I think Nemotron is the most important project that exists,” said Alexiuk, who also uses the pseudonym “Joe Nemotron” across social media. “I’m a firm believer that openness is a very important thing to undertake, so I’m going to be the No. 1 fan of whoever is doing that the best. And that is Nemotron.” https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/ChrisAlexiuk_captions_9MB.mp4 It’s this matter-of-fact directness and affable approachability that makes Alexiuk’s teaching style so appealing. On the social media platform X, he goes by the handle “llm_wizard.” His avatar: a laughing cartoon caricature sporting a slouchy sorcerer’s hat and brandishing a magic wand. It’s no surprise, then, that Alexiuk likens Nemotron to a magical library — its users fellow wizards in search of knowledge that can move mountains. “You’re a wizard in search of prepared spells, and Nemotron has a spell for everything,” he said. “Just choose the one you need.” In non-wizard terms? “There’s a category of model that’s going to be close to the kind of work you want to accomplish,” Alexiuk said, explaining that Nemotron supports that whole ecosystem of AI users: from individual developers using a model like Nemotron 3.5 Lightning for repetitive, high-frequency execution work to a company deploying Nemotron Ultra for long-running autonomous agents, deep research and enterprise tasks. NVIDIAN Chris Alexiuk (left) engages with developers during the Build-a-Claw event at GTC Berlin. “I think that openness helps more people understand AI and hopefully leads to more people doing really ingenious things with these tools at the limit,” Alexiuk said. “If a tool is amplifying skill, it’s amplifying human expression.” From Birding to Model-Building Alexiuk first became fascinated with machine learning in a computational physics class at Trent University in Ontario, Canada. “After that, I learned about TensorFlow and that you could build image classifiers that ran on your GPU,” he recalled. As an initial one-off project, Alexiuk built a classifier that would alert him whenever his friend’s distinctive pet bird, a Yellow-Faced Gray Budgerigar, appeared in frame on his webcam during shared video game sessions. “Because we were playing video games, I wasn’t focused on my friend’s webcam, but I didn’t want to miss seeing the bird when it appeared,” Alexiuk said. “And then my whole life changed, because in that instance I realized it’s crazy what you could do with technology.” Since then, he’s been embedding himself in the open source AI community. “To imagine within the span of a few years going…

articles.title: More Performance From Every Byte: How Full-Stack Codesign Solves AI’s Memory Challenge
articles.content: Larger models, longer contexts and agentic applications are increasing GPU memory pressure while supply tightens and prices rise — a trend expected to continue through the near term. NVIDIA works closely with memory partners to rapidly adopt the latest memory technologies. NVIDIA was first to adopt HBM3e and HBM4 technologies into an accelerated computing stack. But the approach isn’t to simply pack more memory onto the GPU. It’s full-stack codesign. NVIDIA intentionally designs GPUs, CPUs, networking, storage and software together to get more useful work out of memory at every layer of the AI factory. That matters because an AI factory runs on a memory and storage hierarchy. GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) is the fastest, most expensive and most contested tier — with model weights and KV cache competing for limited capacity. Below it sit CPU memory, local SSDs and shared storage, each trading speed for more capacity at a lower cost per bit. How much useful work a byte does depends on how well the whole hierarchy is used: shrinking what must be stored, placing it on the right tier and bringing it back to the GPU before it’s needed. Byte for byte, NVIDIA makes the most efficient use of memory at every layer — and the results show it. From NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra to the Vera Rubin platform, HBM capacity per GPU rose roughly 3%, while agentic throughput per dollar rose by up to 30x on SemiAnalysis AgentX. Agentic Inference Is Putting More Pressure on HBM Frontier models now have trillions of parameters — the values that hold what an AI model learned in training. KV cache, which holds the context the model needs to understand each active request without reprocessing the same information, is also expanding. Agentic trajectories carry prior context across repeated model and tool calls, in some cases processing up to 3 million tokens, so each request’s working memory grows over time. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) adds relevant enterprise information to prompts, creating even more context to process and retain. During inference, HBM primarily holds both model parameters and KV cache. The result: greater pressure on HBM. Why AI Factories Need a Memory Hierarchy Adding more HBM capacity per GPU is the obvious response to that pressure, but capacity delivers only what bandwidth can move. Think of HBM as a warehouse and memory bandwidth as its loading docks. A larger warehouse holds more inventory, but the docks set how much can move in and out at a time. Once the docks are at capacity, moving more inventory takes longer and slows response times. If delays exceed the required service level, the added space can’t be used effectively, even as it adds cost and draws power. That’s also why no operation keeps all its inventory in the closest, fastest space. What’s in motion stays near the line. What’s waiting moves to a larger, cheaper space nearby and returns before it’s needed. An AI factory faces the same limit. More HBM can hold more KV cache and support more concurrent users. Every added user shares the same compute and memory bandwidth. But when each user expects fast responses, eventually memory bandwidth is unable to supply data as fast as compute can use it: a limit engineers call the memory wall. Past that point, extra HBM capacity can’t be put to work, yet it still adds costs and draws power. The data still needs a place to live, but not all of it needs the fastest, most expensive tier. This is why an AI factory manages data across a memory and storage hierarchy. Maximizing the Value of Every Byte With Full-Stack Codesign NVIDIA’s full-stack codesign makes every byte of HBM count by relieving pressure from model weights, KV cache and RAG data. It does this with techniques that each target a different source of inefficiency: Shrink model weights and distribute them across the NVL72 domain. The NVFP4 format reduces the space required for weights compared to FP8, the lowest precision possible on the NVIDIA Hopper platform.…

articles.title: Sony is reviving Stranger Things ‘80s retro hype with new wired headphones — and it’s something you might recognize
articles.content: Wired headphones are having their moment. As we turn to more physical media and collect more vinyl and cassette tapes, we need to get our hands on the best ways of listening to them. Is streaming dying? Well, no, not by any means. But more and more people who have invested in physical media need a way to listen to their music. Anyone you talk to who had a music collection in the '80s and early ‘90s will tell you the same thing — the Sony TPS-L2 Walkman and the MDR-3 changed the audio game. You could take your music with you anywhere and look pretty stylish while listening. In line with the retro audio revival, thanks to a trend of digital fatigue , Sony has reimagined its iconic 1979 headphones with the release of the MDR-3R. The same, but different (Image credit: Tom's Guide) In looks, there’s not much that separates the headphones back then from the headphones now. They’ve had minor upgrades to make them suited to modern music listening, but side by side they look virtually identical. The headphones are featherlight at just 1.3 ounces, making them the lightest headphones in the Sony lineup. They have a flexible headband adjuster, too, to get your ideal fit. They have the same classic earpads that come in blue and orange, with both included with purchase of the headphones. The wire has been updated to have a USB-C input, making it compatible with modern devices. There are also in-line controls with a microphone, making them feel like modern wired headphones without compromising the overall look. Sound quality (Image credit: Sony) You’re likely wondering how these headphones might sound. Since they’re essentially a replica, not much has changed, but Sony says minor adjustments have been made to retain the classic sound and make the headphones suited to more modern music. The MDR-3R headphones keep the classic analog warmth of the originals with a few tweaks. The 23mm driver is based on the 1979 version, but offers a wider frequency range, so the bass is more manageable for the cans. I haven’t listened with these headphones as of yet, so I can’t speak from first-hand experience, but if they’re anything like the Gadhouse Wesley Headphones , we can expect crackly warmth with a nostalgic feel, but these retro headphones have 40mm dynamic drivers. How much do they cost? (Image credit: Tom's Guide) So, how much will these cans be setting you back? Well, they’re actually pretty affordable at $59. They can easily complement the NW-WM1AM3 or the NW-WM1ZM3, Sony’s new Walkman devices. This is also cheaper than other retro-style headphones on the market, since the Gadhouse Wesley Headphones cost $89. Running up that hill (Image credit: Sony) But the exciting headphones launch isn’t all that Sony has in store for us. Fully embracing the influence Max Mayfield has had on us over the last few years, the MDR-3R headphones are also launching in a Stranger Things edition. This design has a black headband with the choice of black or red earpads in the box. These cost a little more at $79, and $20 may seem a little steep simply for a different colorway, but Stranger Things fans will love this ode to the show. articles.title: Accessibility statements now have a home on GitHub
articles.content: Accessibility work often lives in issue trackers, contribution guidelines, audit reports, team knowledge, and conversations with users. When that information has no predictable home, people who encounter a barrier must search for it, and maintainers lose context as contributors and project ownership change. An ACCESSIBILITY.md file, now visible on repository overview pages, gives a project one durable place to explain its accessibility goals, contributor expectations, supported environments, known limitations, and process for reporting barriers. GitHub makes accessibility statements easier to find GitHub now recognizes the ACCESSIBILITY.md file in the repository’s root, .github/ directory, or docs/ directory. A repository can also inherit a statement from its organization’s .github/ repository. For public repositories, maintainers can add or propose a statement from Insights > Community Standards using a concise starter document. GitHub’s community health files help people understand how a project works: Contribution guidelines explain how to propose changes Codes of conduct establish expectations for participation Security policies explain how to report vulnerabilities Recognizing ACCESSIBILITY.md gives accessibility information a dedicated place alongside that guidance. New repositories also include an accessibility issue label by default. The statement explains how to report a barrier and what to expect next, while the label helps maintainers organize and track the resulting work. Accessibility statements make project practices visible GitHub CLI’s accessibility statement , for example, documents settings, known barriers, and workarounds. It explains why table output can be difficult to follow with a screen reader and provides a command that prints pull request numbers and titles one per line instead. It also asks contributors changing prompts or output to show the results with relevant accessibility settings enabled. Developers using the CLI get a specific workaround; developers contributing to it get clear expectations for their changes. The GitHub Annotation Toolkit’s accessibility statement documents a limitation of its Figma library: annotations use canvas position, connecting lines, and matching numbers to visually convey relationships. Access to individual canvas objects does not necessarily communicate what those relationships are. The statement gives collaborators a concrete alternative: provide a structured text description that identifies each annotated element, its intended semantics and behavior, and any relevant ordering. For developers preparing or receiving a design handoff, this explains what information needs to accompany the visual annotations. The file also explains how to report accessibility barriers and explicitly states that the library has not undergone keyboard-only or screen-reader testing. Readers get both practical guidance and clear limits on what the project has verified. Showing this information in the repository overview makes it easier to find alongside the project’s other documentation. Document what the project can maintain There is no one fixed format for an ACCESSIBILITY.md file. A small library, command-line tool, documentation site, and large web application have different users, risks, and maintenance capacity. Start with accurate information that the project can keep current. Priorities and goals: Explain why accessibility matters to the project and which user experiences receive attention. Contributor expectations: Describe the accessibility checks, evidence, or review practices expected for changes, including instructions for human contributors and coding agents. Reporting accessibility barriers: Provide a direct, accessible reporting path. Do not require disability disclosure, screenshots, or recordings. Response process: Explain how maintainers acknowledge, triage, track, and communicate about accessibility issues. If the project uses…

articles.title: Postcards from tomorrow: Powering the agentic era through open source
articles.content: When organizations across the industry first adopted generative AI , most consumed it through a hosted API, but open-weight models are changing that. Models like the Qwen family and GLM-5 are published on model registries like Hugging Face, many under Apache 2.0 licensing, and load directly into open-source serving engines like vLLM and SGLang . “For a growing set of workloads, that gap is small enough that the model is no longer the main constraint.” Closed models pulled further ahead in 2025, but not by much. The Stanford AI Index 2026 put the top closed model’s lead over the top open model on the Arena leaderboard at 3.3% as of March 2026. For a growing set of workloads, that gap is small enough that the model is no longer the main constraint. KubeCon + CloudNativeCon is taking place in Salt Lake City from November 9 to 12. Register now ! Serving a downloaded model is the easy part; the value comes from changing it: fine-tuning on your own data or applying reinforcement learning (RL) against your own tasks, then putting the improved version back into service. That learning loop is where most of the cost and infrastructure complexity sits. Consider an internal coding agent that a platform team builds to fix failing CI builds that runs on an open-weight model pulled from Hugging Face. When a build fails, the agent clones the repository into a sandbox, reads the logs, writes a patch, and runs the tests. Every attempt produces a trajectory, the record of a single run, with a clean reward signal, because the tests either pass or they don’t. Those trajectories feed the learning loop. On a schedule, the team fine-tunes the model on successful fixes or runs an RL job against the reward, then evaluates the new checkpoint and rolls it out behind the existing endpoint. Over time, the model learns how the team’s codebase breaks and how it gets fixed. That one workflow combines three workload types, and each stresses a platform differently. Where a learning loop gets hard Three workloads, three platforms? Inference needs long-running replicas that scale with traffic and start quickly. Fine-tuning and RL jobs are close to the opposite: gang-scheduled across GPUs and run to completion. Agents need short-lived execution environments that spin up fast. Teams that stand up separate infrastructure for each end up with idle GPUs in one place and queued jobs in another, and every handoff adds cost. Untrusted code at high density Agents execute code the model wrote seconds earlier, and a shared kernel is a thin boundary. The CI agent from our example also spends most of its life waiting on a model response or a test run. Giving each agent a dedicated, always-on pod makes isolation expensive, so teams trade security for density. Scattered capacity and slow starts Teams add GPUs incrementally, across regions, and sometimes on hardware they already own on-premises. A training job may fit on capacity that exists but sits outside the cluster, and when inference scales out, each new replica has to load tens of gigabytes of weights before it serves a single request. One control plane for the whole loop Rather than building a separate platform for each stage, treat the learning loop as a standard cloud native systems problem. Kubernetes already reconciles declared state and schedules work. The job is now to extend those primitives to models, agents, and accelerators, giving the pattern three layers on a shared control plane. Model layer: serving and tuning as declarative workloads The model layer covers serving, fine-tuning, and evaluation. Several open-source projects work here, including KServe , llm-d and the Kubernetes AI Toolchain Operator (KAITO) . KAITO represents a model and its GPU requirements as a custom resource and reconciles that state. A model update becomes a change to desired state, not a script someone has to run. articles.title: Microsoft's Imagine Cup 'Evolves' From Student Competition To AI Startup Contest
articles.content: theodp writes: That Was Then: The Imagine Cup competition, Microsoft explained in a 2003 press release, "seeks to provide students [aged 16-and-up] around the world with resources to use technology and Web services to solve everyday problems [...] Imagine Cup is about empowering students to apply their creativity and knowledge toward making the world a more-connected place." This Is Now: "Building is Hard. Selling is Harder." begins the "Why Imagine Cup?" promo video for the 2027 Imagine Cup competition, which is pivoting to an AI startup-first focus in recognition that "A new era for founders is here." "Since 2003, Imagine Cup has empowered emerging innovators to turn ambitious ideas into real-world solutions with Microsoft technology," Microsoft writes of the Imagine Cup Evolution. "Now part of Microsoft for Startups, Imagine Cup enters its next chapter in 2027, opening the competition to eligible early-stage startups and founders everywhere." An Eligibility FAQ drives home the point that Imagine Cup is no longer a student-only competition: "Imagine Cup 2027 welcomes eligible early-stage startups across seven categories; founders do not need to be students." And if you think making high school students compete against seasoned full-time employees of startup companies seems a tad unfair, Microsoft advises: "Eligible student-led startups are encouraged to enter the Student Startup category but may choose an industry category instead." The #1 overall startup will win a $250,000 cash award and $1,000,000 in startup credits. However, Student Startup category entrants are ineligible for the open category prizes (where the 2nd-place winner gets $50,000 cash and $350,000 in credits, while 3rd place is good for $25,000 and $350,000 in credits); they will instead compete for a single prize of $25,000 cash and $250,000 in credits. The Official Rules (PDF) note that all startups must have a valid Azure Subscription ID and a Microsoft for Startups account. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: My new favorite LED light bulb doesn't just change colors, it can also play music — and it's 32% off right now
articles.content: I’ve tested my fair share of smart and color-changing light bulbs over the years, but I wasn’t quite sure about one that doubles as a Bluetooth speaker. After trying out the GE LED+ A21 LED Light Bulb for a month, I was surprised by how well this combination works. Currently, you can get the GE LED+ A21 LED Light Bulb for $22 at Amazon . This LED bulb normally retails for $32, but Amazon is offering an instant $10 discount that drops the price to $22. Given the long-term energy savings of LED bulbs compared to conventional incandescent and fluorescent options, it might be worth grabbing a couple. Here’s why. shop all early Black Friday deals at Amazon The GE LED+ A21 LED Light Bulb Color Changing Bluetooth Speaker lets you play music directly from your phone to it, making it the perfect bedside companion when you're trying to wind down. In addition, it comes with a remote that easily lets you change its colors, intensity, and even set up a multi-unit system for stereo sound. View Deal What really sold me on this setup is that it’s not trying to compete with all the other speakers I have around, including the two Apple HomePods in my bedroom that I use with my TV. While the sound isn’t mind-blowing, it’s more than enough to help me wind down before bedtime. Since the bulb sits in a lamp right next to my bed, it’s perfect for playing ambient noise or an audiobook to help me fall asleep. That same balance also makes it a solid upgrade for a home office, delivering background music while working. John Velasco / Tom's Guide John Velasco / Tom's Guide John Velasco / Tom's Guide John Velasco / Tom's Guide It’s also worth highlighting that despite its color-changing abilities, this isn’t technically a "smart" bulb that relies on Wi-Fi — and you don’t need to download another app. Instead, it pairs with a simple remote that lets me cycle through colors, tweak brightness, and adjust audio playback with the click of a physical button. This plug-and-play simplicity makes it super easy to use and ideal for older adults or elderly family members who don’t want the hassle of complicated tech. (Image credit: John Velasco / Tom's Guide) The reason I suggest getting a pair isn’t just the extra savings — it’s that you can link multiple bulbs together completely wire-free. I’ve set it up so the two light bulbs sit on opposite sides of my bed, assigning one as the left channel and the other as the right. Effectively, I get a true stereo pair that makes listening far more immersive. There’s also a Party Mode that syncs the bulbs to change colors and pulse to the beat of the music. Between its simple remote controls, clutter-free audio, and wire-free stereo pairing, this two-in-one bulb convinced me it’s no gimmick — especially while you can grab it for just $22 for a limited time.

articles.title: Uncommon Thinkers: Curiosity led Mary Brunkow to an immune breakthrough — and a Nobel Prize
articles.content: Mary Brunkow receives her Nobel Prize from King Carl XVI Gustaf of Sweden in Stockholm on Dec. 10, 2025. (Nanaka Adachi Photo) Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners . Mary Brunkow had considered becoming a veterinarian or doctor — she knew she wanted to do good in the world and help people. Then, as an undergraduate at the University of Washington, she stepped into a research lab for the first time. Inside, a professor she admired and his team were using fruit flies to study genetics. “You walked in this door and it was like entering this new world,” Brunkow said, recalling the collaborative, passionate environment. “I just loved it. There was the smell of ether in the air. There was this real love of the science.” After graduating and going on to earn a doctorate, Brunkow built a career in research. She joined Seattle-area startup Darwin Molecular and oversaw a team studying mutant mice afflicted by severe autoimmune disease. The scientists painstakingly identified the responsible gene, which led to valuable insights into the immune system’s T cells. Brunkow worked on other projects at Darwin, too. But after an acquisition and a merger, the company’s local R&D operation shut down. Brunkow moved on. She ultimately landed at the Institute for Systems Biology (ISB) , her immune-system research well in the past. Then, in October 2025, came an unexpected call: She would share the Nobel Prize in Medicine with former Darwin colleague Fred Ramsdell and Osaka University’s Shimon Sakaguchi for discoveries explaining how the immune system avoids attacking the body’s own tissues. Now a distinguished investigator at ISB, Brunkow was stunned by the honor. But Jim Heath, president of the institute, sees it as well deserved. “Mary brings an exceptional combination of scientific rigor, intellectual curiosity, and humility to her work,” he said. “She’s driven by fundamental questions about biology and isn’t afraid to challenge conventional thinking in pursuit of answers.” Beyond her scientific prowess, Heath also praised Brunkow’s efforts to create a workplace as welcoming and vibrant as the one that captivated her as a college undergrad. “She’s a generous colleague who values collaboration and helps create an environment where other scientists can do their best work. She’s deeply committed to creating opportunities for students who will become tomorrow’s scientists,” Heath said. “Those qualities are every bit as important as the discoveries themselves.” Brunkow fell in love with research when she first visited a fruit fly genetics lab at the University of Washington. (ISB Photo) A gene hunt in a janitor’s closet When Brunkow joined Darwin in 1994, the biotech — whose backers included Microsoft co-founders Bill Gates and Paul Allen — was riding a wave of advances from the Human Genome Project, an effort to sequence humanity’s DNA playbook. Darwin scientists sought genes linked to disease that might point the way toward new treatments. “It wasn’t a one-drug company. It wasn’t hyper-focused on something very specific. It was trying to figure out how we can affect change in patients,” Ramsdell said at Life Science Washington’s annual conference in April. One project focused on “scurfy” mice, which carried an inherited mutation that caused devastating autoimmune disease. Researchers suspected the mutation disrupted a crucial regulator of the immune system. Darwin wasn’t set up for mouse research, so Brunkow commandeered a janitor’s closet and began carefully breeding the mice to narrow down the area containing the mutant gene. The work was far more laborious and slow compared to today’s technology, but it was groundbreaking for that period. It delighted Brunkow. “It…

articles.title: Apple Creator Studio App Updates Rolling Out, Starting With Logic Pro
articles.content: Apple today began rolling out the Creator Studio app updates that it announced last month . For example, both the Creator Studio version and standalone version of the Logic Pro app for the Mac were updated today. It is our understanding that Pixelmator Pro will also be updated today, with more apps in the suite set to be updated throughout November. MacStories editor John Voorhees tested the updated Creator Studio apps over the past week and has shared his impressions of the new features. Logic Pro for Mac has received a new Liquid Glass design, an AI-powered Intelligent Assistant feature that can help you build beats using natural language, a redesigned browser that centralizes things from loops and instruments to patches and plug-in presets, an enhanced Stem Splitter that now separates drums, and more. Sidecar support will turn an iPad into a multi-touch controller for Logic Pro on the Mac. Apple says Intelligent Assistant requires a Creator Studio subscription, so that feature will not be available in the one-time purchase version. Here are the Logic Pro version 13.0 release notes for the one-time purchase version, which costs $199.99: Version 13.0 - Unified Browser • Find the perfect sound faster with a redesigned browser that brings your entire library into one place — loops, one-shots, instrument and effect patches, and plug-in presets • Add your own custom or third-party sound to the browser and Logic Pro uses music understanding to analyze and classify them, applying tags that make even massive sample libraries easily searchable • Narrow results with dynamic tag filtering, or describe what you're looking for in plain terms like "atmospheric pad" or "lo-fi kick" • Find similar sounds or samples across your entire collection with ease • Browse your licensed Splice sounds alongside the rest of your library • Add any folder on your Mac as a Browser location for instant access to your personal collection Enhanced Stem Splitter • Break the drum stem into individual tracks — kick, snare, hi-hat, toms, cymbals, and other percussion • Rebalance your entire drum mix without ever needing the original multitracks All-New Liquid Glass Design • Bring clarity to your workflow with translucent surfaces and deeper contrast — menus, toolbars, and windows feel lighter and more refined Sidecar Support • Transform your iPad into a Multi-Touch controller for Logic Pro on your Mac • Tap to trigger cells in Live Loops, populate Step Sequencer patterns, adjust plug-ins and instruments, and control multiple mixer channels at once Play Surface • Play instruments with a resizable performance window — trigger drum and chord pads with your typing keyboard and mouse, or tap your iPad using Sidecar • Play a musical keyboard with controls for velocity, modulation, and polyphonic pitch glide • Make beats by triggering drum pads and use note repeat to add rolls — perfect for trap hats • Customize Chord pads to follow the Chord track in realtime, so every chord and note you play fits perfectly Step Sequencer Multi-Select • Select a range of steps with a drag or Shift-click, then adjust velocity, note repeat, or any parameter for the entire selection at once • Copy and paste groups of steps to new positions or rows, and use dedicated key commands to select all steps in a row, invert a selection, or nudge selected steps Apple has more detailed Logic Pro release notes in a support document . For $12.99 per month or 129 per year in the U.S., a Creator Studio subscription provides access to full-featured versions of Final Cut Pro, Logic Pro, Pixelmator Pro, Motion, Compressor, MainStage, Keynote, Pages, Numbers, and Freeform. One-time-purchase versions of Final Cut Pro, Logic Pro, Pixelmator Pro, Motion, Compressor, and MainStage remain available on the Mac App Store. Free versions of Keynote, Pages, Numbers, and Freeform continue to be available, but they do not receive all of the new Creator Studio features. When the remaining updates are released,…

Sure, buying a chair may not sound as exciting as picking up a new console or a high-spec monitor, but the upgrade in comfort is worth its weight in gold, especially if you're just used to playing from your sofa. That's something you'll definitely want to consider if you're planning a big gaming sesh (say, for the release of GTA 6). With that in mind, I took a look at some of the options that are currently out there. In this article you'll find 12 terrific choices from N-Gen, GTPlayer, Razer, and more. Prices start at under $90, but there are also several higher-spec options available. Grab one of these and enjoy your return to Vice City in style. articles.title: PROLED touchscreen MacBook Pro review roundup: fantastic screen, touch is secondary
articles.content: The first reviews of the new MacBook Pro PROLED with touch display are out. All of them rave about the screen, just about all of wince at the price, and most shrug about touch. Get used to cleaning smudges on the new MacBook Pro's display - Image Credit: Apple Apple says these are the best MacBooks it's ever made, but it always says that. It says these have touch screens, and it's always rejected saying that. Now that the 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR models are in reviewers' hands, there is much talk of how Steve Jobs hated touch screens. Some like iJustine say he had a point, but all say what John Ternus has about this being the right time to add touch. Continue Reading on AppleInsider | Discuss on our Forums

articles.title: Memory makers mint megabucks while buyers beg for mercy
articles.content: The big memory manufacturers continue to print money at the expense of long-suffering buyers, with industry DRAM revenue approaching five times its level a year ago. Demand for datacenter capacity and AI accelerators drove the 369 percent year-over-year surge in Q3 2026, Counterpoint Research reports . "Bit shipments rose only about 4 percent this quarter, yet DRAM revenue reached nearly $200 billion, close to 5x a year ago," says Counterpoint senior analyst Jeongku Choi. "AI has turned memory from a commodity into a valuable scarce resource, and buyers are now competing for supply rather than negotiating on price. With prices still rising, suppliers are on track to set new earnings records again next quarter." As Reg readers will be well aware by now, the AI infrastructure boom has sent demand for server memory soaring. Manufacturers have prioritized more lucrative products for that market, squeezing supplies for PCs, smartphones, and other devices. The consequences have been a sharp increase in memory costs, leading to higher prices of products that use it. The average price tag for a laptop or desktop was up by double-digit percentages across Europe this summer, resulting in falling PC shipments as vendors struggled to secure supplies and buyers were put off by the expense. A similar effect has been seen in the smartphone arena, with shipments down by at least a fifth as rising memory costs squeezed budget models out of the market, leaving vendors to focus on high-end devices instead. Price increases slowed from the steep rises seen in the first half of the year, Counterpoint says, but average DRAM selling prices still reached $1.90 per gigabit and remained the main driver of revenue growth. Of the big three memory makers – the DRAMvirate, if you like – Samsung led with a 38 percent share of DRAM revenue. Separately, it forecast company-wide operating profit of about $80 billion for Q3, up from $9 billion a year earlier. SK hynix posted stronger sequential growth, helping it recover some of the share it lost earlier this year, according to Counterpoint. The firm made a $62.8 billion profit , and predicts that memory shortages will persist until at least 2030. Micron's DRAM revenue grew more slowly than rivals', but its wider business hardly suffered: fiscal fourth-quarter net profit reached $37.7 billion , exceeding its entire second-quarter revenue of $23.8 billion. Counterpoint's research director MS Hwang expects to see memory prices remaining high next year. "[High-bandwidth memory] prices, which lagged commodity DRAM this year, are now catching up. Long-term agreements (LTAs) are supporting prices, and supply will stay tight because major new fabs will not start production until 2028. LTA terms may cause results to differ between suppliers in the short term, but over time they should all follow the same upward trend," he says. That means more bad news for buyers, but more massive profits for the memory makers. ®
articles.author: Dan Robinson

articles.title: Longtime investor Martin Tobias says no to 99% of startups — his new AI tool helps them find a yes
articles.content: Martin Tobias. (Incisive Ventures Photo) Martin Tobias was pitched by about 4,500 startups last year. He wrote 10 checks. Now the pre-seed investor is offering the rest of them a consolation prize: an AI tool that tells founders which investors are most likely to say yes. Tobias, a longtime figure in the Seattle tech scene, is now based in Spokane, Wash. He founded Loudeye, a digital media company that went public during the dot-com boom and later sold to Nokia, and went on to lead biofuel maker Imperium Renewables and group-buying startup Tippr. He was a venture partner at Ignition Partners, an early backer of DocuSign, before starting Incisive Ventures in 2020. The firm closed a $10.5 million fund last year to back early-stage B2B software companies. Investor Match started as an internal tool to help Incisive’s portfolio companies find seed and Series A investors. Tobias said he has 17,000 contacts but can only keep about 150 of them in his head, a limit known as Dunbar’s number. To use the tool, founders upload a pitch deck, and Investor Match returns 20 investors ranked by fit, based on stage, check size, geography and what each firm has actually backed. It also drafts outreach emails, but it doesn’t send them. Most founders send those emails cold, or pass the list to their existing investors and ask for warm introductions, Tobias said. Investors who have accounts on the platform can also respond to founders directly. A free preview shows all 20 matches with fit scores, with the top three fully expanded. The full list costs $20, which Tobias said roughly covers the API costs of running it, about $1,000 a month. Every founder Tobias turns down now gets pointed to the tool. “Just because I wasn’t the right investor for that company doesn’t mean that the right investor wasn’t out there,” he told GeekWire. Incisive appears on the platform like any other investor. Some founders who were matched with the firm asked whether Tobias had tilted the algorithm toward himself. He said he hadn’t, and that he only wants pitches that actually fit. “Just because I wasn’t the right investor for that company doesn’t mean that the right investor wasn’t out there.” Martin Tobias Other companies offer investor matching as part of broader fundraising platforms, including Metal and OpenVC , which Tobias said charge founders monthly subscriptions. He said OpenVC relies on simple keyword matching, while Investor Match uses AI to read each investor’s website, portfolio and blog posts, which takes “millions and millions of tokens.” Some of those companies are trying to build venture-scale businesses off founders’ fundraising, Tobias said. “I think that’s just f—ing evil,” he said. “I don’t think you should try to make money off people who quit their job and are putting everything into trying to raise their first one to $2 million.” Founders have told Tobias they’ve raised more than $100 million from investors they found through the platform since it launched about six months ago, though he acknowledged he can’t verify that because the money doesn’t flow through Investor Match. Investor Match is also an extension of his investing thesis. He said his fund looks for B2B software companies like DocuSign that “reduce friction at scale” by taking a business process and doing it better in software. “That’s exactly what Investor Match is,” he said. “What’s the friction in the market that you’re dealing with? Investors finding founders, founders finding investors. OK, can software help with that? I think it can.”
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser

articles.title: UPERFECT GR14BU portable monitor review: A 120 Hz 3K OLED touch display at a killer price
articles.content: As the portable monitor category matures, a number of new players have entered the market to claim their share of the pie. One company that we haven’t had a chance to sample yet is UPERFECT. But the company is coming out of the gate swinging with the first review sample that it sent our way: the GR14BU. As its name suggests, the GR14BU is a 14-inch portable monitor, but it doesn’t have a run-of-the-mill 60 Hz 1080p IPS panel like you’ll find on most of the best portable monitors in this segment. Instead, it features an OLED panel with a dense 2880 × 1800 (3K) resolution and a 120 Hz maximum refresh rate . On top of that, the GR14BU also supports touch input in Windows 11. On paper, it’s a promising product with a street price of under $300. That’s roughly three times the price of a garden-variety 14-inch IPS panels, but is it worth the premium? Design of the UPERFECT GR14BU At first glance, the GR14BU impresses with its black aluminum frame that wraps around the 14-inch panel. The sleek design is enhanced by the glossy glass, which is typical for OLED panels. Things take a downward turn from there, however. While the GR14BU features an integrated kickstand, which is much appreciated on a portable monitor, it’s tiny and is mounted directly in the middle of the back panel of the monitor. Because of this position, the GR14BU can only be used in landscape mode. Even if you could somehow prop the monitor up in portrait mode, this would be hindered by the two USB-C ports and HDMI port on the right side of the monitor, and the five OSD buttons on the left side. (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Speaking of the OSD buttons, they feel cheap and wobble around like buttons you might find on a cheap plastic stopwatch you’d find at Dollar Tree. They’re shockingly bad for a device with a $399 MSRP. The five buttons are: Power, OSD, Up, Down, and Back. UPERFECT included a plethora of cables and adapters in the box, which should satisfy all your connectivity needs. Our review unit included two USB-C-to-USB-C cables, one micro-HDMI to HDMI cable, two 180-degree USB-C to USB-C adapters, one 180-degree micro-HDMI to HDMI adapter, and one USB-C wall adapter. Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware One thing to note as we discuss cables and adapters is that when connecting the GR14BU to my test system using a single USB-C to USB-C cable, the monitor was locked at 20 percent brightness and would not go any higher. However, when using the second USB-C to USB-C adapter connected to the USB-C wall adapter, the GR14BU would automatically boost brightness to its maximum level. UPERFECT GR14BU Specifications Panel Type / Backlight OLED Screen Size / Aspect Ratio 14 inches / 16:10 Max Resolution & Refresh Rate 2880 x 1600 @ 120 Hz Response Time 1 ms (GtG) Typical Brightness 500 nits Contrast Ratio Typical 100,000:1 Ports 2x USB-C (DisplayPort Alt Mode), 1x micro-HDMI Speakers 2 x 1-watt Touch Support Yes Dimensions 12.2 x 8.5 x 0.28 inches Weight 1.3 pounds Warranty 1 year OSD on the UPERFECT GR14BU The OSD on the GR14BU is no-frills, offering just the basic controls that you’d expect to find on a portable monitor. Without even accessing the main OSD, pressing the Up button brings up the volume controls, with a subsequent press of the Up button raising the volume, while pressing the Down button lowers the volume. Likewise, pressing the Down button separately invokes the Brightness menu. Pressing the dedicated OSD button brings up the full menu, where you can access picture and color settings. Pressing the Up and Down buttons navigates you through the OSD; pressing the OSD button again executes a menu item, while the Back button takes you back one level in the OSD. Display Performance on the UPERFECT GR14BU The GR14BU features a 14-inch display with a dense-for-its-size 2880 x 1600 resolution, in a 16:10 aspect ratio. That pixel-dense panel is backed by a 120 Hz refresh rate, which is twice that of most portable monitors, along with…

articles.title: I broke a working agent seven ways. The metric I was watching caught two of them.
articles.content: In September, I ran two models through the same 20 support tasks. Both scored 20 out of 20. Then I assigned each model two refund requests that the underlying billing data didn’t support: one against an uncollected invoice, and one for double the invoice’s value. Claude Haiku 4.5 issued all six refunds across three distinct permission configurations. Claude Sonnet 5 issued none. Their success rates looked identical, but their behavior diverged completely on the only scenarios capable of causing financial damage. In October, I reran the evaluation harness . This time, the smaller model declined every unauthorized refund. I initially attributed this to queue ordering: the two trap tasks sat at the end of a 22-task queue instead of arriving in isolation, suggesting that processing 20 prior invoice tasks taught the agent to verify state before acting. I documented this theory in a neat report. “Their success rates looked identical, but their behavior diverged completely on the only scenarios capable of causing financial damage.” Then I checked the execution transcripts for the active model alias. In September, the haiku alias resolved to claude-haiku-4-5. In October, the same alias resolved to claude-haiku-5-5. I reran the isolated trap tasks three times against the new model version, and it declined all six attempts. Queue position had nothing to do with the outcome; the underlying model had been silently upgraded behind an unpinned alias. I discovered this only because of a script search I nearly skipped. An unlogged, uninitiated deployment had occurred. Nothing in my high-level success metrics flagged the shift: 20 out of 20 in September, and 18 out of 19 on scored tasks in October (with the single failure stemming from an intentionally ambiguous prompt). Although the silent model update improved performance, the underlying monitoring gap remains concerning: none of the metrics I tracked would have alerted me if performance had degraded instead. I stopped asking whether my agent was functioning and focused on a narrower diagnostic question: If I intentionally break the system, which metrics actually detect the failure? Intentionally breaking the agent The target system is a customer support agent interacting with a mock enterprise API spanning 30 scoped operations across tickets, users, billing, subscriptions, files, and messages. Every API call writes to an append-only audit log, and each task concludes with a state change that an external script verifies mechanically against the database. The suite contains 19 standard scored tasks alongside the two refund traps. I established a baseline using Claude Sonnet 5.5 (claude-sonnet-5-5) with full administrative privileges across three identical runs. Evaluating three baseline replicates is critical: a detection system that fires false positives on an unmodified setup is useless. Every detection threshold reflects the baseline variance doubled to account for real-world statistical distribution. I then introduced eight specific regressions—one per test run—to simulate common production failure modes : Weaker model: Executed the standard prompt using Claude Haiku 5.5. Speed pressure: Added a single instruction directing the agent to minimize API calls and skip optional read operations. Truncated documentation: Restricted the API documentation to list only 11 of the 30 available commands. Missing scope: Revoked one required permission per task from the credential grant. Stale reads: Routed read queries to an asynchronous replica that lagged behind primary writes. Flaky upstream API: Intercepted a deterministic 25% of API calls with transient errors. Slow upstream API: Introduced 1.5 seconds of artificial latency to every network call. Distractor tool: Exposed a deprecated alias alongside the valid close-ticket command that accepted calls without mutating state. Six of these eight regressions execute inside the API behind a per-run wrapper script, ensuring deterministic, reproducible…

articles.title: Intel leaker claims Nova Lake desktop chips have 5.1 GHz clock limit beyond 90°C
articles.content: According to new information from reasonably reliable Intel leaker Jaykihn, Intel's upcoming Nova Lake desktop CPUs will have an unusual limiter applied. He claims that the next-gen desktop parts from Intel will "universally limit the maximum core frequency to 5.1 GHz when above 90°C." That doesn't mean the parts will top out at 5.1 GHz, which would be disastrous, but it does mean that you're going to need some darn good cooling to reach high clock rates on Nova Lake desktop CPUs. Go deeper with TH Premium: CPU (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Intel VP Robert Hallock sets Nova Lake expectations, teases return to Raptor Lake for DDR4 platforms CPU scaling with DLSS Intel's one-two punch plan in desktop CPUs is taking shape Benchmarking AMD's BC-250, offering Steam Machine-like performance at half the price AMD splits Zen 7 into three EPYC families for 2028 and starts selling server CPUs by the agent Let's be clear about what he's saying. He's not saying that Nova Lake CPUs can't go above 5.1 GHz. He's also not saying that Nova Lake CPUs have their thermal limit at 90°C. While Jaykihn doesn't provide any clock rate information, he does imply that the chips will go above that, possibly quite significantly, as long as the thermals are kept in check, and he does say that the "Tjmax" value of Nova Lake is 100°C. Notably, that's a drop from 105°C in Arrow Lake, although prior-gen Raptor Lake CPUs had the same 100°C peak. Preliminary.Nova Lake -S desktop processors will universally limit the maximum core frequency to 5.1GHz when above 90C.This is separate behavior from traditional TJMax thermal throttling at 100C.Alike TJMax, this temperature threshold cannot be shifted upwards. November 4, 2026 The mechanism that this most clearly resembles is Intel's own Thermal Velocity Boost . TVB, if you're not familiar, is the feature that allows high-end Intel CPUs to hit their highest clock rates. Put simply, TVB simply says that if the chip isn't overheating, it can go 100-300 MHz higher than its rated Turbo Boost Max speed. It's a little confusing, because these TVB clock rates are often quoted as the "Max Turbo Frequency"; Intel even does this itself. But TVB clocks are not the same as standard turbo clocks, and a lot of users who don't have exotic cooling probably never actually see these speeds in practice since they do require optimal conditions. Does this mean that the practical limit of Nova Lake desktop CPU clocks is 5.1 GHz? Well, that depends on how hard these parts are to cool. Remember, we're dealing with chips fabricated on a 2nm-class process; in this case, it's reportedly TSMC's N2P for the compute tiles, while the peripheral chiplets are all on Intel's own 18A or 18A-P . This has consequences, as N2P is reportedly much denser than 18A , but it also lacks back-side power delivery, which means that the thermal resistance of the individual dies is considerably lower. Combined with much lower power consumption from a real node step, it may turn out that Nova Lake is actually quite easy to keep cool. Ultimately, that is going to depend in part on how much Intel decides to push the "fMax", or maximum frequency. Rumors have put AMD's Zen 6 desktop Ryzen processors above 6 GHz for peak clock rates; if that's true, Intel could be looking at as much as a 20% clock rate disadvantage at 5.1 GHz. Obviously, as noted above, the chips are expected to have a higher fMax than that, but it remains to be seen how easily users can keep the parts cool enough to make use of the extra clock rate headroom given this new limit. Both Intel's flagship Core Ultra 9 285K and the Red Team's extant Zen 5-based Ryzen 9 9950X can reach 5.7 GHz before overclocking. Intel's familiar eXtreme Tuning Utility (XTU) software gives users full control over TVB, Tjmax, and core turbo ratios. (Image credit: Future) For tuners, a frustrating detail is that this 5.1 GHz hard clock limit apparently "cannot be raised." That means folks doing system tuning on Nova Lake will…

articles.title: From open beta to global GA: What Docusign learned by bringing contract AI workflows to agents
articles.content: Connecting an AI agent to enterprise software is relatively easy. Making sure it can find the right information, carry out the intended task, and stay within a user’s permissions is where things get complicated. That’s what Docusign discovered while developing its Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server, which entered open beta in May 2026 , and reached global general availability on September 30, 2026. “There’s a big difference between building tools and solving actual customer problems.” Docusign CTO Sagnik Nandy The Docusign MCP Server lets compatible AI assistants and agents access select Docusign capabilities to create, sign, and manage contracts without requiring users to switch applications. Someone could ask an assistant to find a contract, check its status, or prepare an agreement for signature, with Docusign handling the underlying work. A human remains ultimately responsible for reviewing and approving the transaction and its outcome. “There’s a big difference between building tools and solving actual customer problems,” Sagnik Nandy , Docusign’s chief technology officer, tells The New Stack . From APIs to AI agents Traditional REST APIs let developers connect applications and automate tasks through predefined requests. AI agents work differently. A user describes what they want in natural language, and the agent works out which tools to use. MCP is an open standard that lets AI applications connect to external data and tools. A server exposes capabilities that a connected AI application can discover and invoke. Docusign wanted to make its Intelligent Agreement Management (IAM) platform available inside the AI tools their customers use, helping organizations create, commit to, and manage agreements. Through MCP, selected Docusign capabilities are accessible from the AI environments customers already use. Docusign announced the open beta at its Momentum conference in New York in May 2026. Preparing it for wider use revealed challenges beyond the early demos. What the beta revealed Nandy says engineers working closely with customers can usually anticipate the prompts they’ll submit and the responses they expect. That gets harder when a wider audience has access to the same tools. “Once you put it out there, you have to really get it right,” he says. “There are different kinds of prompts that come in. The different tools have to work together, both between themselves, but also across our tool boundary and the customer bringing in other tools.” Feedback led Docusign to expand the contract data, workflow actions, and administrative controls available through MCP. “We added support for local files coming in, so a lot of people wanted to upload local data and interact based on that,” Nandy says. That expanded access to information inside Docusign’s Contract Lifecycle Management (CLM) software, the company’s most advanced set of contract-related capabilities built on the IAM platform for customers with the most complex agreement lifecycle needs and added support for local document uploads through the MCP Apps interface in supported clients. That lets users work with documents that are not already stored in Docusign, subject to the client and workflow support available. “We also added account-level settings and options,” Nandy explains. “Adding support for people being able to do certain things or turn off certain things at that level, that was also useful.” On September 4, 2026, Docusign announced plans for global availability, which its release notes confirm began on September 30. By GA, the server supported broader agreement workflows and AI-client connections, alongside account-level administration; local uploads use the MCP Apps interface where supported. Docusign has also reported growing uptake. During its second-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings call, the company said cumulative active accounts…

articles.title: How the new streamhouse architecture solves agentic AI’s data problem
articles.content: AI agents are moving from answering questions to taking action, and to do that effectively, they need to know the state of the business at any given moment. Most data architectures still aren’t designed to support querying subsecond updates across the enterprise, which is why the streamhouse has emerged to address this gap. The streamhouse is a data architecture pattern that continuously delivers the current state of a business to applications and AI agents. A group of data infrastructure companies defined it to provide consistency around an approach many organizations have started to deploy independently anyway. A streamhouse can be built from open-source technologies such as Apache Kafka, Apache Flink, and Apache Iceberg, from commercial products, or from a combination of both. The group behind it, which includes Confluent, Aiven, StreamNative and Ververica, has published an open, vendor-neutral definition at streamhouse.com , and anyone may use the name free of charge. A common definition gives architects and data teams shorthand for what capabilities they need and where they sit relative to the rest of the stack. When a data engineer says “we need a streamhouse,” the CFO and other stakeholders can immediately understand what they mean and grasp the value. A different kind of architecture Most data architectures were designed to support business intelligence, where data is processed in batches for human analysis. The lakehouse does that job well and remains the right foundation for it. Agents need something different: data that reflects what’s happening now, delivered at machine speed. “Agents need something different: data that reflects what’s happening now, delivered at machine speed.” That calls for an architecture that continuously captures, processes, governs, and serves a real-time view of the business, so that applications and agents can act as events occur. Use cases include order fulfillment, claims processing, underwriting, and fraud detection, all of which rely on real-time data from multiple sources. A claim might draw on policy records, payment history and customer interactions, and joining those sources as events happen is where the architecture is most valuable. Hyper-personalization in e-commerce and gaming are other examples. What defines a streamhouse? The open definition sets out three attributes. First, a streamhouse is real-time. Data stays current as events occur, rather than being refreshed on a batch schedule. Second, it’s production-native. Analytical systems often lack the fault tolerance and service levels required for operational systems, because they were never intended to power the business. A streamhouse sits in the path of business-critical applications and agents, so it has to meet the same standard as those systems. The third attribute is decentralization. A centralized model ingests data into one place and transforms it there, making it difficult and costly to reuse for anything besides analytics. A streamhouse transforms data to make it discoverable and contextualized, so that data produced once can be consumed many times by agents, applications, and dashboards alike. Shaping data for AI Freshness is one part of the problem, but data shape matters too. For decades, enterprises stored every fact exactly once in highly normalized relational tables. Storage was expensive, and normalization protected developers from update and deletion anomalies. As a result, many domain relationships are encoded in tables made up of little more than two foreign keys. That structure means very little to an AI model. “…many domain relationships are encoded in tables made up of little more than two foreign keys. That structure means very little to an AI model.” Consider an agent that drafts a follow-up email after a customer places an order. It needs to be certain that the customer lives at a particular address and just ordered a particular…

articles.title: Micron's $4.5 billion Taoyuan plant construction halted amidst labor dispute
articles.content: Micron has paused construction on its Fab 11E site at Taoyuan as the company and its Taoyuan labor union have failed to reach an agreement regarding clearer profit-sharing terms. Bloomberg reports that activity on the site has all but halted, except for minor safety work, with some sources saying that executives are concerned about uncertainties regarding negotiations with its workers. The company hasn’t released a statement about the move but has already informed local officials about the suspension. “Taiwan plays an important role in Micron’s global footprint, and our operations today continue as normal,” Micron said. “We are confident in maintaining business continuity for our customers.” The company has recently announced a bonus that could give as much as five times the annual salary of some eligible workers, and has also wrapped up a deal with the bigger Taichung union, although some members say they were dissatisfied with the outcome. On the other hand, the Taoyuan union is still holding out for better terms, with the two parties set to meet again on November 6. It even launched a one-day strike last month to show the chipmaker its resolve and how its operations could be disrupted if it does not meet their demands. Workers from the big three memory chip manufacturers — Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix — have been protesting recently and demanding a bigger slice of the massive profits that these companies are currently making from the AI memory chip boom. SK hynix has recently agreed to pay staff $50,00 apiece , with each employee set to receive $477,000 in bonuses this year and up to $900,000 next year. Samsung Foundry workers also fought for a $340,000 average bonus , which received approval at the last minute and averted a massive strike that would have disrupted the company’s operations. Employees from these South Korean companies expect to nab performance bonuses of up to $400,000 and are rejecting coveted overseas training programs in favor of cold, hard cash. While the company hasn’t made a statement regarding the suspension of work on its Taoyuan site, it’s hard to believe that the move happening so close to its next meeting with the Taoyuan union is a coincidence. It should be noted that Micron is also developing other sites across the world, with plans for an HBM fab in Japan , a $24-billion development on the way in Singapore , plus facilities across the U.S. Nevertheless, the company says it is looking forward to reaching an agreement with the workers, with the Taiwan government hoping for a win-win outcome for both parties.
