articles.title: ‘Hogwarts Legacy’ Gets a Magical NVIDIA DLSS 5 Upgrade on GeForce NOW
articles.content: Hogwarts Legacy receives an NVIDIA DLSS 5 upgrade with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering today, bringing lifelike lighting and materials to the wizarding world on GeForce NOW . Blizzard Entertainment’s World of Warcraft: Forever also opens a new chapter in Azeroth, with a launch-week access reward available for GeForce NOW members. Meanwhile, Ubisoft brings fresh challenges with expansions for Tom Clancy’s The Division 2 and Anno 117: Pax Romana . It’s all part of a packed month of play, with two-dozen games joining the GeForce NOW library throughout November, including eight this week. Hogwarts in a New Light NVIDIA DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering arrives in Hogwarts Legacy today, giving members a new reason to return to Hogwarts, streaming from Steam, Epic Games and Xbox with Play Anywhere support. Published by Warner Bros. Games under the Portkey Games label and developed by Avalanche Software, Hogwarts Legacy is an immersive, open-world action role-playing game set in the 1800s wizarding world. Begin as a fifth-year student, encounter magical creatures, brew potions and learn spells while exploring both recognizable and unfamiliar places. The update adds lifelike lighting and material detail while retaining underlying geometry and textures. Avalanche Software has tuned the integration through DLSS 5’s developer controls to maintain the game’s artistic intent and style. Hogwarts Legacy also includes support for the DLSS Multi Frame Generation and Ray Reconstruction features, accelerating and enhancing the ray-traced graphics that immerse players in Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry. Thanks to NVIDIA DLSS 4.5 controls in the cloud, members can fine-tune their experience. Ultimate members can experience the update with GeForce RTX 5080-class performance across PCs, Macs, handhelds, browsers, mobile devices, compatible TVs and more, without an expensive PC upgrade or waiting for game downloads. GeForce NOW handles the installs and updates, saving the storage space for everyday essentials. Just pick up the wand, hop on a broom and take flight. A New Chapter, Forever Familiar roads. New discoveries. Blizzard Entertainment’s World of Warcraft: Forever launched Wednesday, Nov. 4, and is streaming on GeForce NOW, inviting players into a reimagined original Azeroth built to keep growing for years to come. Explore new and expanded zones, discover gameplay enhancements and take in upgraded graphics in a world where community and the journey take center stage. Access is included with an active World of Warcraft subscription or Game Time, giving returning heroes and newcomers a fresh starting point. GeForce NOW also supports CurseForge Addons for World of Warcraft: Forever , giving premium members more ways to customize their experience. At launch, GeForce NOW plans to support around 100 of the most popular CurseForge add-ons, with the selection evolving to reflect player favorites. Members can request additional add-ons through in-app feedback for consideration in future updates. The cloud keeps the next quest within reach across supported devices. For new World of Warcraft users who don’t already have a subscription, a launch-week access reward is available across all GeForce NOW membership tiers. The access period runs through Wednesday, Nov. 11, at 11:59 p.m. PT. Eligible members can sign in to their GeForce NOW account and head to the Account Portal to redeem while supplies last, on a first-come, first-served basis. Gather the party and venture forward. New Missions, New Horizons From city streets to Roman roads. Ubisoft brings two new downloadable content releases to the cloud this week, sending agents into an overgrown New York and governors toward a new province of the Roman Empire. Launched earlier this week, Tom Clancy’s The Division 2: Echoes of Central Park is the biggest experience since Tom Clancy’s The Division 2: Warlords of New York , opening up Central Park and the Upper West Side for the first time in…

articles.title: Dropbox Plans $350M AI Infrastructure Deal With Tigris Buy, Its Biggest Acquisition Yet
articles.content: Dropbox announced Thursday plans to acquire Tigris Data for $350 million in a transaction the company told Crunchbase News would mark its largest acquisition since its founding in 2007. Founded by former Uber engineers, Sunnyvale, California-based Tigris is building a network of localized data storage centers that it claims can meet the distributed compute needs of modern AI workloads. Tigris has raised about $31.9 million since its founding in 2021, per Crunchbase data . Its October 2025 Series A brought in $25 million from lead investor Spark Capital , with participation from Andreessen Horowitz and Basis Set Ventures . Earlier backers include General Catalyst . Co-founder and CEO Ovais Tariq told TechCrunch at the time of its Series A that the startup had grown 8x every year since its founding in November 2021. The planned deal would give Dropbox a storage platform built for developers whose applications run across multiple cloud providers. A push into AI infrastructure The acquisition news coincides with what San Francisco-based Dropbox describes as “a significant shift” in its AI strategy as it expands beyond storing and sharing files into selling the infrastructure that companies use to build AI applications. Publicly traded Dropbox also unveiled DBX Agent Cloud, which will initially offer standalone object storage — a way to store and retrieve large collections of data, including images, video and the files used to train and run AI models. For Dropbox, buying Tigris offers a faster route into a market that serves a different audience from the individuals and businesses that use its file-sharing software. “Tigris brings together a product already running in production, an experienced team, and established relationships with AI developers,” Eric Webster , Dropbox’s chief business officer, told Crunchbase News via email. “That combination would accelerate our entry into infrastructure for AI applications through DBX Agent Cloud.” A bigger bet amid a slower deal pace Dropbox has made 35 known acquisitions, according to Crunchbase, with much of that activity taking place in its earlier years. Between 2012 and 2015, the company conducted 23 publicly reported acquisitions, including nine in 2014 alone. In contrast, it made four acquisitions across 2024 and 2025, averaging two per year, roughly 65% below its earlier pace. Its recent purchases suggest a focus on AI-powered productivity, search and security. Dropbox acquired scheduling startup Reclaim.ai and document security company Nira in 2024, followed by Promoted.ai and Mobius Labs in 2025. While the planned Tigris purchase would be its largest yet, Dropbox has made other sizable purchases over time. Its acquisitions of e-signature company HelloSign in 2019, document-sharing platform DocSend in 2021 and business forms provider FormSwift in 2022 had purchase prices of $230 million, $165 million and $95 million, respectively. Two paths into AI Dropbox’s push into AI infrastructure is one part of a broader strategy that also includes adding AI capabilities to its existing file-sharing product. For existing customers, the company is bringing AI directly to their Dropbox files to help them find, understand, create, edit and organize content, according to Webster. Customers can switch between supported AI models and work with their Dropbox files in tools like ChatGPT and Claude, with results returning to Dropbox. For companies and developers, meanwhile, DBX Agent Cloud extends Dropbox’s storage capabilities to the infrastructure behind AI applications and agents. “DBX Agent Cloud opens a new developer and infrastructure market for Dropbox, while AI inside Dropbox is intended to deepen engagement, retention and expansion among existing customers,” Webster said. articles.title: Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras
articles.content: The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza , it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing. A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse. In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out. “It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are. Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona. Václav Široký During totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study . In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona. And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that. A Mathematician’s Path to Solar Eclipse Photography Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas , an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one. An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field. Miloslav Druckmüller He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens . articles.title: Apple MacBook Pro (14-inch, M6) review: Speedy M6 chip slips into comfortable shoes
articles.content: It’s that time of the year again, which means that Apple has released yet another refreshed 14-inch MacBook Pro using a legacy chassis. While it looks the same as last year’s M5 models on the outside, it has some key hardware upgrades underneath that address performance and connectivity. This time around, we have a MacBook Pro using the new M6 chip that was first introduced in the refreshed Mac Mini . In addition, Apple has outfitted the MacBook Pro with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 connectivity courtesy of the in-house Apple N1 chip. Thanks to industry-wide price hikes on memory and storage, Apple’s 14-inch MacBook Pro now starts at $1,999. Design of the MacBook Pro (M6, 14-inch) Apple has been using the same design for its entry-level MacBook Pro since 2021, and there are no changes this year (if you want a slightly refreshed design, check out the touch screen-enabled 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pros). It’s still a good-looking laptop, but it’s showing its age. Our MacBook Pro review unit came finished in silver instead of space black. While space black looks great, it’s a fingerprint magnet, so many people might prefer the lighter finish, which better hides your skin oils. The notch at the top of the display now seems archaic, especially after seeing the Dynamic Island on the pricier MacBook Pros. The notch is always staring back at you, even though I have mostly gotten used to it over the years. The main thing going in the notch’s favor is that it resides in the same space as the menu bar, which limits the visual annoyance. Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware My only other niggle with the design is one that I’ve harped about in previous MacBook Pro reviews: the cutout in the keyboard deck that aids in lifting the lid has sharp corners, which can jab your palms while typing. As with previous MacBook Pro generations, you’ll find three Thunderbolt 4 ports (Thunderbolt 5 is not available on M6 models), a full-size SDXC card reader, HDMI 2.1, a 3.5 mm audio jack, and a MagSafe 3 connector. Our 14-inch MacBook review unit measures 12.31 x 8.71 x 0.61 inches and weighs 3.4 pounds, the same as last year’s model with the M5. For comparison, the Gigabyte Aero X16 measures 14 x 9.9 x 0.78 inches and 4.2 pounds, while the Dell XPS 14 comes in at 12.19 x 8.26 x 0.6 inches and weighs 3 pounds. This is the same configuration as the Mac Mini that we reviewed in September, except that our laptop review unit includes 16GB of unified LPDDR5x memory compared to 24GB. Rounding out the specs is a standard 1TB SSD. Slow and steady wins the race in silicon advances. In every productivity benchmark, our M6 MacBook Pro not only outshone the previous-generation M5 MacBook Pro , but it also trounced the prosumer Gigabyte Aero X16 (AMD Ryzen AI 7 350) and Dell XPS 14 (Intel Core Ultra X7 358H) Windows 11 laptops that we pitted it against. articles.title: Microsoft fixed Excel 2016 copy-paste bug. Then reintroduced it. Now it's fixed again
articles.content: The Excel copy-and-paste bug is back, which means Microsoft is making a second round of fixes. The bug first appeared in the September update and manifested in multiple versions of Excel as a silent failure of the paste operation. Users copied content and attempted to paste it, but the destination cell was unchanged no matter how hard they mashed the Ctrl+V keys. Microsoft fixed it in mid-September. But it made a comeback in Excel 2016 when users installed October's security update . Microsoft has now released a new build of Excel 2016 to address the reintroduction of the bug: build 16.0.5574.1006. The company wrote: "The new build includes all security updates for Microsoft Excel 2016, and also fixes the issue that was reintroduced in 16.0.5574.1005, in which paste operations might fail if the workbook contains conditional formatting." Microsoft did not explain how the bug slipped back in. Copy and paste is, after all, a niche bit of functionality. Users reported the recurrence of the bug in October after the KB5002934 update was applied. Rolling back the update resolved the problem until Windows Update pushed the patch again. KB5002934 is a security update that resolves glitches including remote code execution and information disclosure vulnerabilities. The problem affects only Excel 2016 and is not the result of the latest Windows security update. Rather, it was reintroduced in an Excel update delivered through Windows Update. A user in a Microsoft Excel forum said the issue had appeared on workstations throughout their organization. "What's frustrating is that this is the same issue we encountered before, which was supposedly fixed in a previous update. Now it's back, barely a few weeks later." And now, at least, it appears to be fixed once again. Still, if Microsoft is determined to reintroduce bugs into Excel, perhaps it might also be tempted to bring back the Hall of Tortured Souls (a secret first-person 3D mini-game hidden inside Microsoft Excel for Windows 95) and populate it with the testers who managed to miss the issue's resurrection. ®

articles.title: Postgres and ClickHouse can share tables. EnterpriseDB wants one set of rules to govern them.
articles.content: If you have built anything that needs both a system of record and fast analytics , you know the shape of the problem. Postgres ® holds the orders, the accounts, the state your application cannot afford to get wrong. ClickHouse software answers the questions. A row store tuned for transactions was never built to answer at speed: what happened across a billion events in the last hour, which cohort is churning, what the agent should do next. Both engines are excellent at their jobs. The misery lives entirely in the gap between them. “Both engines are excellent at their jobs. The misery lives entirely in the gap between them.” EnterpriseDB (EDB) has acquired Altinity, the independent company behind Altinity Stable Builds, the Altinity Kubernetes Operator, and Altinity.Cloud. The headline is corporate. The reason a developer should care is narrower: The #1 contributor to Postgres and the people who have run ClickHouse software in production for nearly a decade now work on one roadmap, and that roadmap is aimed at three pains you live with every week. Pain 1: The CDC job is the product nobody asked for Count the moving parts between a committed Postgres transaction and the same row being queryable in ClickHouse software. A replication slot. A connector with its own failure modes. A message broker you size, secure, and patch. A sink that must survive schema changes without silently dropping columns. A dedup strategy, because at-least-once delivery means duplicates. Monitoring on every hop, because lag in any one of them turns a “real-time” dashboard into a lie. None of that code is your product. All of it is on your on-call rota, and it is the reason the page comes at 3 a.m. Pain 2: Your agent is reasoning over last night’s data Agentic workloads changed the economics of staleness. A dashboard 20 minutes behind is annoying. An agent that approves a refund, reprices inventory, or flags a transaction on a 20-minute-old aggregate is wrong, and wrong at machine speed, thousands of times before anyone notices. “An agent that approves a refund, reprices inventory, or flags a transaction on a 20-minute-old aggregate is wrong, and wrong at machine speed…” So developers building agents write the same awkward code: Query Postgres for current state, query ClickHouse software for the trend, stitch the two in the application, and hope the clocks agree. You have become the integration layer, and the integration layer is where the bugs live. Pain 3: You run the stack twice Every row-level rule, masked column, and “analysts see aggregates, not customer IDs” policy exists once in Postgres and again in ClickHouse software, and the two drift the first time someone updates one and forgets the other. Operating ClickHouse software on Kubernetes is its own job: Keeper, storage classes, replica placement, backups, upgrades, and one or two engineers who have quietly become “the ClickHouse people.” And if you took the shortcut of a managed analytics service, your data lives where the vendor says and your bill scales with their pricing model, not with your infrastructure. Two engines, two permission models, two operators, two support contracts, and a lock-in you did not choose. Read against those three pains, the deal starts to make sense: Each one maps to a pillar of what EDB and Altinity now plan to build together. Pillar 1: One shared layer, not a pipeline Today, Postgres, WarehousePG (EDB’s MPP warehouse), and ClickHouse software can read the same Apache Iceberg tables and query each other. Postgres writes the record and ClickHouse software reads it through the same open table format, with less data movement and integration effort between them. What is planned is one shared catalog and one governance model across all three engines, and one sovereign control plane for Postgres and ClickHouse software. articles.title: Dropbox ditched AWS S3 for its own in-house system. Now it’s buying Tigris to sell S3-compatible storage to AI developers.
articles.content: Dropbox is entering the AI infrastructure space in a big way, announcing plans on Thursday to acquire Tigris , a startup that provides object storage for AI applications. The cloud-storage giant tells The New Stack that it’s paying $350 million for Tigris, a move designed to accelerate Dropbox’s own ambitions in selling storage infrastructure to developers and businesses. Indeed, alongside the acquisition news, Dropbox also announced DBX Agent Cloud, an upcoming offering that will initially let developers purchase object storage directly from Dropbox. Dropbox, it’s worth noting, is no stranger to building storage infrastructure itself. Kicking off in 2015, the company moved more than 90% of its user data off Amazon’s S3 cloud storage service onto an in-house system dubbed Magic Pocket , in a bid to improve performance and reduce costs. But as Dropbox chief business officer Eric Webster explains, selling storage infrastructure to external customers presents an entirely different set of challenges. “Operating infrastructure for Dropbox and offering a storage product to developers involve different requirements,” Webster tells The New Stack . “Tigris brings a working commercial product, an experienced team, developer relationships and early customer traction.” “Tigris brings a working commercial product, an experienced team, developer relationships and early customer traction.” That “customer traction” includes a slew of companies such as Amplified, Railway, Runpod, and Replicate, spanning everything from developer hosting platforms to GPU infrastructure and AI model deployment. Precisely the kinds of businesses that need fast, reliable access to large volumes of data, often while running applications and AI models across different environments. Eye of the Tigris Chief architect Yevgeniy Firsov flanked by CTO Himank Chaudhary (left) and CEO Ovais Tariq (Credit: Tigris) Founded in 2022 by former Uber engineers Ovais Tariq (CEO), Himank Chaudhary (CTO), and chief architect Yevgeniy Firsov , Tigris has built an S3-compatible storage platform that allows developers to keep their data accessible across different cloud and compute environments. For developers training AI models, that could mean storing large datasets in one place while renting computing power from multiple providers. Using Amazon S3 in such situations can incur additional data-transfer costs, known as egress fees, and delays, particularly when the computing happens outside AWS. Tigris addresses this by automatically keeping data close to where it’s needed, while charging no egress fees for transfers out of its storage service. The company announced a $25 million Series A round of funding in October 2025, with investors including Spark Capital and existing backer Andreessen Horowitz. While much of Tigris’s appeal lies in its existing product, customers and developer relationships, Dropbox sees an opportunity to turn that foothold into a much bigger business in the commercial storage infrastructure market. “Combining those strengths with Dropbox’s experience operating storage at scale would give us a faster path into this market,” Webster says. “The acquisition lets us build on what both teams have already developed and learned from their customers.” And so one of the clearest expressions of that ambition is DBX Agent Cloud, a service through which Dropbox plans to sell storage infrastructure to developers building AI applications, with Tigris expected to provide the underlying object-storage technology if the acquisition passes the usual array of regulatory approvals. But why is Dropbox making this push into AI infrastructure? And why now? “AI applications are creating and working with growing volumes of content, from images and video to training datasets and model artifacts,” Webster says. “As models and compute providers change, that…

articles.title: Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display review: The screen that every Mac deserves
articles.content: Apple's fans know all about waiting. The company tends to polish features, especially in hardware, that some other laptop vendors release faster. The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display ends the wait for two long-requested elements: OLED and touch, both on the platform for the very first time. That comes at a price. The 16-inch version we have on review starts at $3,399 and is $7,899 as configured. 14-inch systems start at $2,899. Those are $400 bumps over the existing MacBook Pros with identical chips, making the OLED panel a pricey upgrade. But those who can afford these high-end systems will get the best display on a Mac, if not laptops in general. Add in a significant reduction in weight and improved speakers, and you're getting a lot of small tweaks that add up over what was already one of the best laptops , even if many of the aesthetics haven't changed. Design From a distance, this new MacBook Pro doesn't look all that different from the existing models, which are still on the market, which may upset some people looking for a more sweeping redesign. They come in the same colors (space black, like our review unit, and silver) and they largely have the same design. Technically, the new OLED display stack allows for a thinner system, but our 16-inch review unit, at 16 mm thick, is just 0.8 mm shorter than an equivalent 16-inch MacBook Pro with Liquid Retina screen. Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware The aesthetic differences show up once you open the laptop. For one, the notch in the display is gone with the PROLED XDR models, replaced with the Dynamic Island from the latest iPhones. Let us rejoice; while the notch never bothered me on phones, it always felt in the way, dipping into the macOS menu bar. This isn't perfect, but it feels far more natural and has added functionality (see "Dynamic Island and macOS Touch Features" below). Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Then there's the glowing Apple logo on the back of the lid. We haven't seen this for years, and while I could take or leave it, it's definitely going to make some fans nostalgic. The old glowing Mac logos used light from LCD backlights, getting the effect with no extra power. Because OLED panels only light up pixels when they're needed, Apple is making an aesthetic choice to power the logo with a bit of extra electricity this time. The glow matches the brightness of the display, which is a fun touch. I didn't see anything in settings to disable it. Apple's bezels are thinner, which has let Apple stretch the display to 16.3 inches on this new 16-inch model (it's still 14.2 inches on the smaller one). The displays are now rounded on all four sides. On the Liquid Retina displays, they're rounded on top to match the curves in the chassis, but are squared on the bottom. It's not a huge change, but it does cut some pixels on the bottom of the screen and looks a bit like an iPad. Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Otherwise, the system looks largely the same. You have the same ports: MagSafe 3, two Thunderbolt 5 ports, and a 3.5 mm headphone jack on the left; and an SD card reader, an additional Thunderbolt port, and HDMI output on the right. But the OLED laptop feels different when you pick it up or put it in a backpack. Changes to cooling in the new 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR and the switch to an OLED screen get the laptop down to 4.1 pounds with M5 Max (4.0 pounds with M5 Pro), whereas the Liquid Retina versions are 4.7 pounds. You can really feel the half-pound difference. (The 14-incher is down from 3.5 pounds to 3 pounds, too.) And that's lighter than some of its new competition, too. Microsoft's Surface Laptop Ultra with Nvidia's RTX Spark chip is 4.4 pounds and thicker at 0.75 inches. The Lenovo Pro 9n, also with RTX Spark and its own OLED screen, is a lighter 3.64 pounds and is thicker at 16.7 mm. (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) There has been talk of a sturdier hinge, but it does still wobble when you touch it. No one has gotten around that issue. Comparing it to…

articles.title: 'Stop dirty datacenters': Europe-wide protests planned demanding building moratorium
articles.content: Campaigners against datacenter expansion are planning two days of coordinated action across Europe on November 6 and 7, demanding an immediate moratorium on new large-scale developments. Following the US midterm elections , where restrictions on massive AI server farms were prominent in the campaigns from candidates in both major parties, it's now Europe's turn. Over 100 groups across 15 European countries will protest the boom in bit barn building over the next couple of days. As well as demonstrations, there will be public meetings, stalls, petitions, walking tours, cycle rides, poetry readings and other creative actions, the organizers say. The coalition of groups has put up a website – stopdirtydatacentres.eu – with an interactive map allowing anyone to find information on the events taking place and where. In the UK, there is a photocall planned at 8am on November 6 outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) in Whitehall Place in central London, but also a Community Day of Action the following day at London's Brick Lane, where a facility is planned on the site of the former Truman Brewery. Also on November 7, there will be a "family event" at St Michaels & All Angels Church in Great Torrington, Devon, to highlight the massive 1.5 GW data campus and on-site battery energy storage that is planned for 850 acres of farmland near the town. The planned actions are a response to growing concerns about the impact of the wave of new compute shed projects on local communities, public infrastructure, land, water and energy use, housing, jobs and the cost of living. Such concerns won't have been helped by recent events, such as a Google subsidiary reportedly felling 250,000 trees illegally in Finland to clear the ground for a server hall. The campaigners claim that governments, the European Union and the tech giants are gambling with the future by racing ahead with server farm developments without proper scrutiny of the environmental, democratic and social impacts they might have. A recent report found that businesses and private-sector trade associations dominated meetings with UK ministers to discuss datacenters, while environmental groups didn't get a look-in. Campaigners are calling for an immediate moratorium on new large-scale projects across Europe, until clear frameworks are in place to determine whether new facilities should be built and under what conditions, with proper scrutiny and meaningful public participation. "Datacenter developers in the UK and Europe want to cash in on the AI goldrush whatever the consequences. But communities everywhere are fighting back, seeing through Big Tech's PR machine and calling this what it is – a massive grab of scarce land, water and power resources by Silicon Valley billionaires," said Oliver Hayes, Head of Campaigns at Global Action Plan (UK). "With governments failing to answer very basic questions about how many datacenters we need, what for, where, and how pollution will be avoided, the only reasonable course of action is an immediate moratorium," he said in a supplied remark. They are unlikely to get much sympathy from the British government, which has pegged its hopes for economic growth on AI and wants more bit barns built to fulfil this. It has already used its powers to overturn rejections of planning permission for server farm projects by local councils. Omdia analyst Alan Howard argues that datacenters also became a convenient political target during the US campaigns. "The datacenter industry took a big hit in the US midterm elections which is quite disappointing, but not that surprising," Howard told The Register . "The anti-datacenter rhetoric accelerated 12 months ago and in the last six months skyrocketed. While there have been many catalysts to point our fingers at, datacenters turned into an opportunistic political football. To be blunt, there is no shortage of politicians willing to exploit any opportunity to win an election and the datacenter…

articles.title: The Download: Texas’s fragile AI boom and energy policy shifts
articles.content: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Texas was the new epicenter of the AI data center buildout. That might be kaput. Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech’s largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position. Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat, Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor, and Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. They won after making data centers a central issue on the campaign trail. The swings could spell trouble for hyperscalers with ambitious plans in the state. They also add to growing anxiety that America’s AI buildout could stall. Here’s how the election results could reshape AI’s future . —James O’Donnell What’s next for US energy policy after the midterm elections? Democrats have taken control of both the House and the Senate, but we probably won’t see major federal climate and energy legislation while Trump remains president. The midterm elections could, however, be a big deal for energy at the state and local level. The results could shape everything from the state grid and data center development to renewable energy and greenhouse gas emissions. Find out what the midterms could mean for the future of US energy . —Casey Crownhart This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday. A new bill could change how the US builds energy infrastructure A sweeping bit of legislation designed to cut red tape could speed up the buildout of energy infrastructure in the US. On November 9, the Senate is set to vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). It’s a plan that could start an overhaul of the slow, complicated process for getting energy projects approved. But some environmental groups oppose the bill, or parts of it. Explore the trade-offs behind America’s proposed permitting overhaul . —Casey Crownhart The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 America’s data center boom has hit a political wall Voters opposed them in 40 of 41 midterm ballot measures. articles.title: Motorola's new Signature 27 has it all if you can stomach the $1,600 price tag
articles.content: Motorola is patching a hole in its US lineup with a non-folding flagship phone, but the pricing puts this device dangerously close to the company's expensive tablet-style foldable . The long-rumored Motorola Signature 27 is real, featuring top-of-the-line specs, a super-bright OLED screen, and a ton of cameras. But all this high-end hardware won't come cheap in the age of AI. Motorola's new flagship smartphone will run a whopping $1,600 when it arrives later this month. The Signature 27 is a completely new take on flagship smartphones from Motorola, leaving behind the middling legacy of the Edge series. However, you'll still immediately clock this as a Motorola device due to its distinctive use of materials and Pantone colors. The phone is metal, ceramic, and glass, but the backs are textured polycarbonate. The device comes in Coal Smoke (black) or Capulet Olive (green) colors. The former has a "tactical weave" finish inspired by automotive design, and the latter is "textile-inspired." This device will include the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, the most powerful mobile chip Qualcomm offers right now. While some smartphones have flirted with 16GB of memory, that's less common these days. The Signature 27 will have 12GB like Samsung's base model flagships. However, there's not going to be an upgrade option for more. You will, however, get a generous 512GB of storage. Read full article Comments

articles.title: Anthropic won't fix a Claude Dispatch flaw that could let attackers execute remote commands across corporate boundaries
articles.content: A vulnerability in Anthropic’s Claude products lets any browser extension that can control Claude Dispatch make Claude Desktop run code on the computer – or even a different machine signed into the same Claude account – with no browser exploit and minimal user interaction required. Anthropic, aware of the problem since May, has taken no action to close the hole. Dispatch is a feature in Claude that lets users send and manage tasks from their mobile phone or browser to Claude Desktop, an AI agent that runs commands on their computer. Forever Security researcher Gal Weizman discovered that Claude Dispatch’s interface and API were reachable from an ordinary logged-in web session at claude.ai. So a browser extension able to control claude.ai could send commands to Claude Desktop as if they came from the legitimate Dispatch user. “That extension was able to perform a classic escalation of privileges. Because now Claude has access to the files in the operating system, it can run code on the operating system and compromise the machine completely,” said Weizman. “We’re talking about millions of installs.” Claude.ai received about 950 million monthly visits as of mid-2026, and Cowork usage included 1.2 million sampled sessions from more than 600,000 organizations during May, according to Anthropic’s usage data. Weizman found and disclosed the Claude Dispatch flaw, dubbed ThisBash, to Anthropic, and shared his research exclusively with The Register . The AI company acknowledged his report as a valid vulnerability in May, but closed the security issue as a duplicate of a known flaw it was already tracking. Anthropic did not pay Weizman a bug bounty or issue a CVE, but told him it planned to retire Dispatch at the end of October. That didn’t happen. The Claudefather did not respond to The Register ’s questions – including when it planned to retire the feature – but as of October 30, the official Claude support page listed Dispatch as available in limited beta on some Pro, Max, and Ultra plans, but not available to new users. “If you already use Dispatch, you can keep using it for now,” the page reads . Even if Anthropic does kill off Dispatch, Weizman says the fundamental flaw in Claude’s design still exists, and the security weakness now lives on in other features like Claude Code Remote Control and Claude Cowork sessions. The researcher told us he communicated all of this to Anthropic. “They still decided not to do anything about it,” Weizman said. “Claude Cowork is now accessible via the web version, and it shares the same sessions as you can access in the desktop version,” he said. “Once again, using an extension, you can use the Cowork sessions to say: ‘Please access this file and grab it. Please install this malicious npm package. Please run code on the operating system.’ And it would.” Weizman said his research “started with a vulnerability. And it ended up being a design choice that enables this attack vector very easily.” There is a prerequisite for this attack to work: A browser extension with access to claude.ai must be present. But, as Weizman explained, that’s not very difficult to achieve. How the attack works An attacker could trick someone into installing a malicious extension – but it’s typically easier to just hijack a legitimate one. Weizman told us hijacks of this sort "happen a lot, whether by classic supply-chain compromise, or a black market for buying legitimate extensions." Next, users must be authenticated to both Claude on the web (claude.ai), and Claude Desktop with the Dispatch feature enabled. “But given the Cowork session discovery, and the Code remote-controlled session discovery, there's much less need for opting into the Dispatch feature specifically,” Weizman said. In a subsequent technical report and video proof-of-concept exploit, Weizman outlines the six steps in the attack chain. articles.title: Making Immersive LLM Chat Experiences More Accessible
articles.content: I have had the privilege of helping to improve the accessibility of multiple immersive LLM chat experiences in the course of my career. Now I want to share this knowledge with you. Accessibility is a core part of a functional digital experience. As the LLM chat pattern continues to spread like wildfire across the web, we risk excluding people if these experiences are not built with accessibility as a core consideration. It is also worth re-mentioning what “exclusion” means here : It’s the loss of knowledge, the loss of opportunity, the loss of utility, the loss of employability, the loss of entertainment, and more. What Is An Immersive LLM Chat Experience? “Immersive LLM chat experience” is a catch-all term for full-screen experiences like Claude , ChatGPT , GitHub Copilot , Gemini , America.gov , Glean , and other similar websites and web apps: The majority of what this post covers applies to both web apps and native apps . This is because these experiences are typically built using web technologies, then placed in a native wrapper via frameworks such as Electron or Tauri . Immersive LLM chat experiences are not patterns such as a pop-up chat, inline text generation utilities, or summarization tools. These simpler applications of LLM technology will have different considerations and expectations. Instead, this is a starting point for making those other experiences accessible. Reframing There is nothing special about chat-based UIs when viewed via the lens of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines . They are interactive experiences, built using web technologies. The losses I’ve described — and the legal liability associated with them — are access barriers in the same way any other web content can be an access barrier. I would also like to mention the social model of disability here: the idea that exclusion can be created by the built environment. For example, consider an elevated entryway that uses a gently sloping ramp in place of stairs. Built environments also extend to digital experiences , and the social model also applies here. The main activities undertaken to operate an LLM chat are already well-established: Inputting text and submitting it, and Reading content and taking action on it. It is how we facilitate — or fail to facilitate — those interactions that’s the salient bit. Visual Bias Before we get into the technical aspects, we must consider the overwhelming visual bias that permeates software creation . We live in a highly visual culture, so our outputs unconsciously reflect and reinforce that. What we need to do here is be aware of and think through the non-visual considerations . While not all disabilities are blindness or low vision conditions, a lot of the core interactions of an LLM chat do need specific accommodations for these two types of disability. Recall the social model of disability here, and how it applies to the main flow of using an LLM-based chat. You: Type some words into an input and send it as a message, Wait for the LLM to parse your message, then Read the message the LLM generated. Let’s demonstrate at a high level what someone who can fully see the screen experiences compared to someone who uses a screen reader and cannot see the entire screen, or large portions of it: ( Large preview ) Visually, we can see the LLM reply appear. Someone who uses a screen reader does not know new content has appeared because: Their focus is still on the input that sent the prompt. No non-visual mechanism is present to signal new content showed up. So, how do we create an experience for someone who uses a screen reader that is equivalent to the experience of someone who can fully see the screen? To start, we use live regions . Use Live Region Announcements Live region announcements will enable someone to know what the LLM has responded with without having to move focus from the input used for prompting . articles.content: Apple has largely stopped making users join a waitlist to access its Siri AI assistant. According to an updated Apple support document , Siri AI "will begin to download automatically" once users opt in, but the waitlist is now reserved "during time of high demand," and wait times can vary. articles.content: Apple has informed App Store developers that they can now add retention messages sooner, when they want to remind cancelling subscribers of how great their app is. articles.title: See Apple's Touchscreen MacBook Pro in Action
articles.content: Apple enlisted British musician Labrinth to create a new song during an overnight livestream, demonstrating the new touchscreen MacBook Pro and Logic Pro at Apple Tower Theatre in downtown Los Angeles. The session, titled "Labrinth Live on Mac," is now available to watch as a replay lasting almost four hours. It started on November 4 at 8 p.m. Pacific, or 11 p.m. Eastern, with Labrinth tasked with creating a song from scratch. He can be seen reaching onto the ‌MacBook Pro‌'s display to manipulate Logic Pro's mixer controls, with a multitrack arrangement visible onscreen. Viewers were invited to submit questions as he worked, and the finished song is due for release on Apple Music next week. Apple initially teased the collaboration on TikTok with a white box bearing Labrinth's name and instructions to leave it unopened until November 4. Music production was among the uses Apple demonstrated when it unveiled the new MacBook Pro last week. Logic Pro includes an onscreen keyboard, chord pads, and drum pads that musicians can play by touch, including playing multiple notes at once. Labrinth is a singer, songwriter, and producer known for solo releases including "Jealous" and "Earthquake," as well as his music for HBO's "Euphoria." He also forms the group LSD with Sia and Diplo. The ‌MacBook Pro‌ with PROLED XDR Display features a tandem OLED touchscreen and M5 Pro or M5 Max chips in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes. The machines launch on Friday, November 6, with U.S. prices starting at $2,899 for the 14-inch model and $3,399 for the 16-inch model. articles.title: Sector Snapshot: Construction Robotics Funding Soars To $1.6B, Tripling Previous Peak
articles.content: Construction companies are struggling to find enough workers. For startups, that means venture investors are pouring money into companies betting that robots can help close the gap. Companies spanning construction and robotics have raised about $1.6 billion this year through Oct. 29 — more than 4x the $389 million recorded in all of 2025 — according to Crunchbase data. The surge was driven by three companies that raised the majority of the funding. The broad trend: For contractors struggling to hire, the appeal of construction-oriented tech offerings is straightforward: They need to get work done and there aren’t enough skilled workers to do it. The AI-driven data center building boom is only adding to that competition for workers. Labor shortages remain the biggest cause of project delays, according to a recent survey by the Associated General Contractors of America and NCCER . Some of the technology is already at work on job sites. San Francisco-based Bedrock Robotics , this year’s largest funding recipient in the sector, said in August that excavators equipped with its autonomous systems were operating without human operators on commercial projects in Texas and Nevada. The numbers: With roughly two months left in the year, funding has already surpassed the previous five years combined. Companies spanning construction and robotics raised about $1.6 billion through Oct. 29, 3x the previous high of $506 million in 2021, according to our dataset that goes back to 2018. This year’s total is also more than 3x the 2021 high of $506 million. So far, the funding surge reflects much bigger bets rather than more deals. The sector has recorded 30 rounds this year, compared with 28 in all of 2025. Bedrock alone accounts for $870 million across two deals — more than half of this year’s total. This underscores just how much a few large financings are impacting the recovery. Austin-based Icon , which builds homes using 3D printing, also raised two rounds in 2026. It has raised nearly $800 million since its 2017 inception. A company spokesperson told Crunchbase News that the company has taken its technology from an experiment to “an in-the-field system that can build faster, with fewer people, less waste, greater design freedom and lower cost.” To date, the company has built more than 270 homes and structures across five states and two countries. It says that it’s on pace to grow revenue by 4x this year. “Early on, the question was whether a robotic construction system could build a good home,” the spokesperson wrote via email. “Today, the question is whether a company can deliver at volume, across geographies and project types, and improve its economics with each build. That’s only answerable with time in the field.” Notable deals Bedrock Robotics was the largest funding recipient in 2026, impressively raising $870 million across two rounds. The 2-year-old company, which converts existing heavy construction equipment into autonomous machines, announced a $600 million Series C in October led by CapitalG and Emergence Capital . That round, which valued Bedrock at $4.1 billion, followed a $270 million Series B in February led by CapitalG and Valor Atreides AI Fund . Austin-based construction technology company Icon also raised two rounds, bringing its listed 2026 funding to $265 million. Its largest financing was a $200 million Series D in October led by Baillie Gifford and BlackRock , following a $65 million Series C in March. Another $200 million round went to Gravis Robotics , based in Zurich, Switzerland, which develops technology to retrofit construction machinery for autonomous earthmoving and excavation. SoftBank led the company’s Series A in August, which valued the startup at $1 billion post-money. Beyond those large financings, investors backed companies automating homebuilding and specific construction tasks. articles.title: Agility Robotics' Nasdaq debut invites scrutiny of humanoid robot market
articles.content: Humanoid robots remain unproven at scale and have not yet achieved widespread commercialization, compared with industrial robots that have decades of proven track records in warehouses and factories. That frank acknowledgment is among the risks outlined in a securities filing by Agility Robotics—the first dedicated developer of humanoid robots to become a publicly traded company in the United States. The robotics company, headquartered in Salem, Oregon, previously became the first to achieve full-time commercial deployment of humanoid robots at a customer warehouse in 2024. Now, Agility’s public listing on the Nasdaq stock exchange as of November 5 has come with financial disclosures detailing how the company plans to build a business around renting out or selling humanoid robots to perform manual labor. “When we are doing robots as a service, it is much lower risk for customers to use it because they are getting a return on investment on day one,” Jonathan Hurst , co-founder and chief robot officer at Agility Robotics, told Ars. "Because they're paying a rate that is comparable to the human labor rate, and that makes the economics pretty straightforward.” Read full article Comments

articles.title: Bluesky was right all along and will accept your apology any time
articles.content: Bluesky is a niche Twitter-clone frequently accused of being an echo chamber for progressives. After the blue tsunami of this week’s midterms, however, its inhabitants don’t seem to be echoing themselves so much as the vast majority of American voters. The sheer scale of Democrats’ victory is staggering. They won control of both chambers of the U.S. Congress, flipping Senate seats in seven states Trump carried in 2024—including Republican stronghold Texas, which now also has a Democratic governor and attorney general. All in all, this year’s midterms represent the biggest electoral shift in state-level politics to hit the U.S. in generations. They also represent a Texas-sized validation of the worldview Bluesky has become notorious for over the past two years. Amusing how if you read X, Facebook, most of NYTimes and The Atlantic, all of The Argument, and so forth, yesterday was a huge surprise and you have to reset everything from the past two years.But if you joined BlueSky in November 2024 and clicked on any politics-related starter pack, you're good. — Max Kennerly (@maxkennerly.bsky.social) 2026-11-04T11:27:40.179Z BLUESKY WAS RIGHT ALL ALONG — John Scalzi (@scalzi.com) 2026-11-04T04:19:19.671Z Although it officially launched in the spring of 2023 , Bluesky might as well have been born on election eve in 2024. That was the moment millions of disillusioned Twitter users decamped from a website owned by the largest single contributor to Trump’s reelection. Bluesky quickly became a haven for Twitter expats and grew at a frenetic pace . It went from 9 million users in September 2024 to 15 million by mid-November , eventually reaching its current 47 million. Because many of Bluesky’s users arrived out of principled opposition to X, formerly Twitter, the two sites have arguably existed in opposition to each other. Both portray their counterpart as out of touch, with Bluesky alleging Elon Musk’s algorithm tweaks have skewed X’s political vortex too far to the right, and X suggesting Bluesky is a bubble of liberals who can tolerate anything except a difference in opinion. The latter idea seemed to largely prevail. In 2025, Washington Post columnists , tech world figures like Mark Cuban , and myriad other pundits dismissed Bluesky as smug, self-righteous, and irrelevant. It was the fantasy sandbox where progressives went to play among themselves, protecting reality dwellers from having to hear their drivel. ( “Like a containment dome over a nuclear reactor,” as the writer Josh Barro put it.) So, how well did Bluesky’s users stay in touch with reality between elections, compared with X’s exponentially larger population? Consider the post-midterms perspective. Rather than accept the narrative that 2024 represented a rejection of “wokeness” and a political realignment toward Trump, the manifestly trans-friendly Bluesky suggested the election was more a referendum on postpandemic inflation and global anti-incumbent bias . As an emboldened Trump then proceeded to antagonize U.S. citizens and the rest of the world , while making billions for himself in crypto , Bluesky meticulously chronicled the state of play. It became the premier destination for seeing radicalized older white ladies , abysmally attended pro-ICE rallies , and complaints about the lack of mainstream news coverage around massive No Kings protests. Any random day would find endless posts with evidence that, per the motto of the political philosopher and Bluesky power user Olúfẹ́mi O. Táíwò, “We are going to win.” — Andrew Lawrence (@ndrew.bsky.social) 2026-09-08T01:17:36.844Z Above all, Bluesky proved to be less a bubble than an expression of the multitude of ideological factions that had united under the umbrella of non-MAGAness . . . to argue with one another. Meanwhile, X’s millions of liberal and progressive folks were often drowned out by an algorithm that seemed to favor right-wing voices and their preferred narratives. A bubble chart from Nate…

articles.title: Amazon teams up with Uber on restaurant delivery, years after shutting down its own service
articles.content: (Amazon Image) Amazon is bringing Uber Eats inside its own app, letting U.S. Prime members order restaurant delivery without a separate Uber account and skip the delivery fee on orders of $25 or more. The deal replaces a Prime perk with Grubhub, which Amazon made an ongoing benefit in 2024 after a one-year trial. Amazon said in a statement to GeekWire that it has ended that agreement after identifying “an opportunity to deliver an even better restaurant delivery experience.” The new Prime benefit covers hundreds of thousands of restaurants in nearly 10,000 U.S. cities and towns, from major metros to rural communities. Orders are placed with existing Amazon logins and payment methods, on Amazon.com or in the Amazon Shopping app. Amazon says Prime members could save more than $175 a year through the delivery fee waiver and Prime-only promotions, which it notes is more than the $139 annual cost of Prime. Service fees still apply, the company confirmed. New users get $20 off their first two orders of $25 or more within 14 days, and Prime Visa cardholders earn 5% back on Uber Eats orders through Dec. 5. Members who already pay for Uber One, which includes $0 delivery fees, keep those benefits. But Amazon said the two memberships operate independently, and the Prime perk applies only to Uber Eats orders placed through Amazon. The deal marks Amazon’s latest approach to restaurant delivery. The company shut down its own Amazon Restaurants service in 2019, four years after launching it in Seattle and expanding to more than 20 U.S. cities. Uber had listed Amazon as an Uber Eats competitor in its IPO filing earlier that year. The service let Prime members order meals through its website or the Prime Now app. Amazon cut jobs on the team in early 2018, closed the London service later that year, and also shut down Daily Dish, a workplace lunch delivery service it launched in 2016. The Uber deal is part of Amazon’s broader push to add value to Prime. In February, the company made its Alexa+ AI assistant free for U.S. Prime members . Last year it ended a program that let members share free shipping with someone outside their household. “We’re excited to connect our restaurant community with new Prime fans, while giving Prime members a seamless way to enjoy great food from restaurants through Uber Eats,” Andrew Macdonald, Uber’s president and COO, said in a statement. Members can share the Uber Eats benefit with one adult in their household through Amazon Family.

articles.title: NASA Announces X-70 Experimental Aircraft to Advance Flight Research
articles.content: NASA has unveiled the X-70 Fractal, a new crewed experimental aircraft "designed to accelerate the development and testing of advanced aviation technologies." From a press release: The crewed X-70 features advanced, rapidly reconfigurable flight-control technology that will allow NASA to explore aircraft maneuverability in ways never before demonstrated in crewed flight. The aircraft can also accommodate up to 2,000 pounds of experimental payloads in internal and external locations, enabling a wide range of research and flight-testing opportunities. The X-70 Fractal has a takeoff weight of 10,000 pounds and is designed to cruise at Mach .75, reach altitudes of up to 45,000 feet, and provide an operational range exceeding about 1,726 miles (1,500 nautical miles). These capabilities will enable NASA to conduct demanding flight research across a broad range of operating conditions. The X-70 joins a storied legacy of experimental aircraft that have helped establish America's leadership in aviation. From the Bell X-1, which first broke the sound barrier in 1947, to the X-15 hypersonic research aircraft and today's X-59 quiet supersonic demonstrator, NASA has spent decades pushing the boundaries of flight. With the X-70, NASA will expand its capacity to conduct experimental flight research, accelerate the testing of emerging technologies, and advance the next generation of American aviation. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: How to get early access to Android’s smart new scam shield
articles.content: When it comes to Android security , we’ve got three main types of threats to contend with as informed phone-owners determined to keep our data safe. First, there are the theft-related worries — the breaches that happen when someone physically takes possession of your device and manages to get past its virtual gates. (Setting up Android’s native theft protection options and enabling all the right Android security settings in advance makes a massive difference in terms of proactive protection.) Next, there are the many, many theoretical threats played up by companies hoping to sell you over-the-top security software. (Choosing a device that actually gets timely and reliable software updates and then maintaining a teensy shred of common sense is generally all that’s needed to keep these overhyped boogeymen at bay.) And finally, every single one of us faces the most worrisome threats of all — the ones related to good old-fashioned trickery and our own occasional lapses in judgment. From phishing to smishing and vishing and now even quishing (I swear I’m not making these up), there’s no shortage of shenanigans trying to trick us into willingly giving up our information without even realizing it. And all the easily accessible AI these days only makes matters worse . Suffice it to say, that last category is generally the most pressing — ’cause it’s our own very human shortcomings that make it possible. And even the most savvy and cautious creatures among us can be convinced to click a thoroughly cloaked questionable link in the right moment. With that kind of threat, your best bet is simply having as many layers of protection as possible in front of you — so if your own guard is ever down and a particularly convincing scam attempt appears in front of you, there’ll be something standing between it and you that says: “Hey buddy: You sure you want to do this?” That’s precisely what’s popping up as an easily overlooked new option on Android right now — in one of the places where you’re most likely to encounter scam attempts on your phone. And as a smart and sensible Android Intelligence reader, you don’t have to wait for Google to officially give it to you to start embracing its power. [Get level-headed knowledge in your inbox with my free Android Intelligence newsletter — a single useful new tip every Friday.] Hello, Enhanced Protection The arena at the center of our attention this week is none other than texting and the de facto default Google Messages app for Android. Google Messages has long had a simple spam protection option among its many buried features , but Google’s in the midst of expanding that to include an even meatier Enhanced Protection mode for all of your incoming messages. Specifically, Enhanced Protection includes three new forms of in-message scam defense: An AI-powered analysis that puts messages from new, unknown senders under an especially strong microscope to seek out signs of “novel and sophisticated attacks” — a trend that Google says increasingly gets hidden within “slow-burn conversations” designed to get you to give up innocuous-seeming but potentially problematic slivers of personal info along the way. An even stronger form of link scanning that looks at real-time signals to see if any link you’ve received contains scammy elements or signs of phishing within — even if the site itself isn’t immediately known to be shady. More prominent warnings anytime you’re about to open a link from a potentially questionable sender — to confirm you actually want to proceed and make sure you didn’t tap something inadvertently. All these new features work from a privacy-first perspective, according to Google, with either on-device processing or cloud-based computing that occurs only in an encrypted, secure dedicated space that makes all the related info inaccessible to anyone else (including even Google itself). The Messages Enhanced Protection options are available for anyone to opt into as of this moment — but, as is so…

articles.title: Apple VP Tom Boger on MacBook Pro weight, design, and the return of the glowing logo
articles.content: Almost everyone in tech already knows about Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, a light, bright, thin pro Mac notebook with a reference-grade touch responsive display, adding a touch of iPad to the Mac. It’s already being talked about as the future, at least of the company’s pro laptops. I spoke with Apple’s Vice President of Mac and iPad Product Marketing, Tom Boger, to find out more. The specs of the new MacBook Pro are written about everywhere — including here — so I wanted to get a feel for how Apple thought about building the system. We looked at the weight the team took out, the restraint behind its design choices, the illuminated logo it brought back, and why the Mac makes so much sense for the enterprise. Weight: a thousand small decisions The first thing people notice about the new MacBook Pro, Boger said, is how much lighter it has become. The 14-inch model is about half a pound lighter, and the 16-inch about 0.7 pounds lighter. This weight loss was not easy to achieve. The team looked at every single component used in the Mac to find opportunities to reduce its weight, Boger said. “It’s not one thing here, one thing there. It’s a thousand things.” The challenge is to reduce the weight of individual components while leaving each part as functional as it was. “You have to make sure you’re not compromising the integrity of whatever component you’re taking the weight out of.” I pictured engineers shaving away microns, milligrams, and grams from all the components used. “That’s literally what it takes,” Boger said. Of all the things Apple did with this product, he said, this was probably the one where “you really have to sweat every little detail.” Design: raise the bar, don’t change the Mac The display is the headline feature of this MacBook Pro, Boger said. It did not appear overnight. Apple’s display engineering team is “one of, if not the best in the world,” he said. Building a panel like this “takes years of development.” The technology is only half the job, manufacturing it at scale is another. He was blunt about the result: “There’s literally nothing else in the industry like this,” he said, pointing to the display’s 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. In working on the project, the question the team kept asking was simple: “If this is the world’s best pro notebook, how do we make it even better?” Apple made it better with an astonishing display. The tandem OLED panel combines two stacked electroluminescent-emitting layers to deliver that extraordinary contrast ratio, up to 2,000 nits of brightness, and self-emissive pixels to eliminate the blooming and halo artifacts you see on other displays. I’ve been lucky enough to see one of these Macs in action alongside a higher-end Windows laptop with touch, and you can very quickly see the difference. Apple has published a helpful white paper to explain more on its display tech. The touch functionality supported by the display follows a similar logic of adding without disrupting. Drawing inspiration from the iPad and iPhone, which almost every MacBook Pro owner already has, the intention was to ensure that the expanded user interface did not fundamentally change the nature of the laptop. “The MacBook Pro is still first and foremost about a trackpad and keyboard interaction,” Boger said. The aim is familiarity from one device to the next. What is new, he said, is pairing touch with a far more powerful system than an iPad Pro, which “opens doors” for creative applications. He pointed out that Apple’s touch is more responsive than on other laptops. You’ll also be impressed at how little the display wobbles when you touch it. The new Mac comes as a new generation of professionals who have used touch all their lives graduate into employment. These digital natives use touch every day, and now they can do so with their Mac. articles.title: Playful wants the masses to start vibe coding
articles.content: Mike Harrington and Darrin Massena think that making an app with AI is still too hard. While you can ask Claude or ChatGPT to build something for you, that demands at least some awareness of programming frameworks and hosting options. AI app builders like Replit and Cursor also aim to be professional-grade development tools for businesses, not something you’d use to quickly scratch a personal itch. Harrington’s and Messena’s startup, Playful , wants to bring vibe coding to a much broader audience. With a handful of simple prompts, Playful will build web-based apps and games that you can push to your phone and share with friends. Users can create up to two apps for free and use them for up to 30 days, at which point the service requires a $10 per month subscription. [Photo: Playful] “It’s for an audience that is less technical, for an audience that until recently didn’t even understand that they could make apps,” Harrington says. Playful isn’t the first company to try bringing AI app creation to mainstream audiences. The highest-profile example is Wabi , which raised $20 million last year to be the “ YouTube of apps ,” though it has since pivoted to be more of an app-powered personal AI agent (while raising another $55 million ). The App Store is also awash in apps like Vibecode , Vibecoder , and VibeStudio , which look to varying degrees like they were made with AI themselves. Harrington and Massena, who worked together on Microsoft Bob and later sold their photo editor startup Picnik to Google , are betting that a combination of social sharing features and their own expertise in software development will help Playful break through. Harrington also cofounded Valve Software, where he worked on the hit PC game Half-Life . The duo launched their startup in 2023 under the name Hatch , intending to offer a no-code platform for web apps, and pivoted to artificial intelligence after realizing how it would make app creation much more accessible. “We’ve always gone after things that are consumer-oriented, and fun, and to a certain kind of audience,” Harrington says. “Picnik . . . grew from just a little photo editor to where we had 60 million monthly uniques, and about 85% of them were women. It’s just a market that people didn’t go after, and I think there’s a similar thing in apps.” [Image: Playful] How Playful works Creating an app in Playful starts with a simple question: “What kind of app do you want to make, and who’s it for?” What happens next is where Playful distinguishes itself from a typical chatbot. Based on your original prompt, it will ask follow-up questions on things like the features you most care about and how you’ll use the app. For instance, I asked Playful to build an audio transcription app that cleans up the text, identifies speakers, creates topic shortcuts to skip to, and lets you tap on the text to hear the corresponding audio. Playful in turn asked about recording scenarios—interviews, lectures, or personal voice notes—and whether I’d want to do things like access old interviews or export full transcripts. “It helps you with the process because it understands a lot of things about apps, making apps, what might make sense, what’s popular in apps,” Massena says. After a few minutes, Playful presents a smartphone-sized app that you can run through Playful’s own app or turn into a standalone icon on your home screen. The apps are web-based, so they work on any device, without distribution through any app store. Behind the scenes, Harrington and Massena say that Playful uses a variety of large language models to fulfill users’ requests. Compared with using a more general-purpose AI tool, Harrington says Playful has more specific training on the process of creating apps and how to distill users’ requests. It also has built-in tools for things…

articles.title: A new bill could change how the US builds energy infrastructure
articles.content: A sweeping bit of legislation designed to cut red tape could speed up the buildout of energy infrastructure in the US. With the dust barely settled on this week’s momentous midterms, the Senate is set to vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on November 9. It’s a plan that could finally start an overhaul of the slow, complicated process for getting energy projects approved, as part of something called permitting reform. People on both sides of the political aisle have been pushing for this type of change for some years. The key question is whether this will cut greenhouse-gas emissions from the US energy sector or push them higher still. The federal permitting system is designed to protect the environment against industrial pollution from large projects like power plants, transmission lines, and natural-gas pipelines. Today, permitting is governed by a range of laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act. And if there’s one thing you might know about the current state of permitting in the US it’s that it’s slow and incredibly complicated. So in its 417 pages, BAAJA attempts to tighten things up. The bill has provisions that narrow the sorts of projects that need to apply for federal permits and others that enact deadlines in hopes of speeding up a process that today can take years. (There are also specific provisions about transmission planning, mining, and the rest of the kitchen sink; this thing is dense .) One thing to know about this bill is that it’s largely technology neutral: It opens the doors for the buildout of projects involving both fossil fuels and renewables. So there’s a weird mishmash of legislators and outside groups supporting it. The bill’s four sponsors in the Senate are two Republicans and two Democrats. The White House has backed this permitting reform bill, with its Council of Economic Advisors finding that it would reduce review times and have economic benefits like boosting GDP. Clean energy groups like the American Clean Power Association have largely come out in favor of the bill too, with the group’s analysis finding that it could unlock 350 gigawatts of new clean energy for the grid. Some environmental groups, however, oppose the bill, or parts of it. An assessment from the Natural Resources Defense Council says the parts about transmission could have substantial benefits for the grid, but the narrowing of environmental reviews could be damaging for public and private lands. Many in the climate world have long been calling for permitting reform, arguing that renewables stand to benefit more than fossil fuels. The thinking is that solar and wind power are some of the cheapest sources available today, so if we unlock the ability to build more energy, they are likely to win out economically. A few early analyses have tried to quantify just what BAAJA would mean for emissions in the US. One, from the think tank Rhodium Group, found that in the best-case scenario, the bill would cut economy-wide emissions by 4%, reduce annual energy bills by $78 per household, and add 200 gigawatts of new clean energy by 2040. In the worst case, emissions would stay about the same. Another report , from the nonprofit research group Resources for the Future, found that the bill could cut power-sector emissions 6% by 2041 and save more than $350 billion on system costs by midcentury. But there are some concerns that this permitting bill’s real effect would be to open the floodgates for new natural-gas plants. As data centers have put more pressure on the grid, a wave of such plants have been announced. “You get down to a trade-off between essentially growing the clean electricity industry on the one hand and then, as a compromise, growing the fossil-fuel industry on the other,” says Kevin Kircher, an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue. To quantify that trade-off, Kircher also modeled the potential emissions effects of…
