articles.title: Gen Z is souring on dating apps. This very NSFW one is booming
articles.content: Connie Collins, a 25-year-old sex educator, walked through the unlocked door of a stylish apartment in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, to find a man lying naked and face down on a bed. “I put on a strap and just started strapping away at him,” she says. “It was just super crazy. I’ve never done anything like that before.” The pair didn’t know each other’s names, nor had they seen each other’s faces. Though they’d later develop a brief friendship, they had met only hours earlier, under pseudonyms, on an app named Pure, billed as “the open-minded dating app.” Even as mainstream dating apps scramble to respond to dwindling subscriber s and Gen Z skepticism, 12-year-old Pure—which presents itself as an alternative to traditional services like Hinge and Tinder, and as an even less inhibited version of kink-friendly Feeld —has been on a tear. In February, the company reported that it had reached $100 million in annual revenue. Pure tells Fast Company that it has now reached . . . a $220 million run rate—and is forecasting to double that figure next year. Over the past year, Pure’s revenue has more than doubled in the U.S, its biggest market. The sex-forward dating app is free to download but men and nonbinary users must pay for a subscription ($13.99 a week, $648 a year) to initiate chats and maximize their visibility. Women have access to most features on the app for free, though the Pure Queens subscription (starting at $4.99 a week) gives them access to more controls. Pure says that its users are split 60-40 between men and women—and most are Gen Z and millennial. (Tinder, which appeals to the same demographic, has a ratio of roughly 75% male, 25% female.) “People are getting a bit tired of all the traditional swipe-based dating apps and they’re looking for something different,” says Pure’s CEO, Luka Dremelj. He credits Pure’s success to its unique interface and user experience. Users on Pure don’t swipe through profiles, accepting and rejecting matches. Instead, they scroll through a feed of “personal ads” posted by other users, expressing interests, desires, or provocative come-ons. That feed is full of individuals who have identified similar turn-ons—everything from music and massage to one-night stands, foot fetishes, and dominant and submissive relationships. Though it facilitates in-person connections, Pure is just as much about chatting and sexting, allowing users to share explicit photos and videos, which disappear after viewing, and engage in video calls. As dating apps contend with Gen Z users who are either uninterested or too anxious to meet in person, Pure offers a different proposition: allowing them to explore their sexuality behind a screen, with limited human contact. The app’s unorthodox approach to privacy—all users are anonymous, even to the app itself, which doesn’t verify identity—is one of its biggest draws, reducing barriers to connections and letting people explore their turn-ons without inhibition. But, as a recent lawsuit in Texas indicates, it may leave some users exposed. A new design language Pure’s approachability starts with its design language, which is filled with bright colors and playful, hand-drawn illustrations after a redesign earlier this year. “We’re bringing this human touch to the user experience,” says Dremelj, who joined the company in 2022, shortly after RM Equity Partners, a European private equity firm, bought the app. “There’s a bit of humor in there.” [Image: Pure] Users first experience this humor during the onboarding process. They begin by choosing their gender and sexuality on screens that feature whimsical drawings. Then they create their “ad,” which serves almost like an old-school newspaper personal, enticing people to click on their profile, which can be customized with photos and different background colors and designs. To make it easier for users to share their desires, Pure allows them to select from a list of more than 20…

articles.title: The midterm elections’ biggest loser? Data centers
articles.content: Data centers were on the ballot this election, and they lost. While results from the midterm elections are still coming in, as of November 4, 38 out of 39 restrictions on data centers had passed—from temporary moratoriums on new construction to full bans. And multiple candidates who made opposition to data centers a key part of their campaign also won. Take the example of William Lawrence , the Democratic candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives in Michigan’s purple 7 th Congressional District, which Trump narrowly won in 2024. Lawrence, a progressive community organizer and cofounder of the Sunrise Movement , was new to politics and faced a challenge running against the Trump-backed incumbent, Tom Barrett. In the primary, facing two establishment Democrats who had raised more money, Lawrence won in part because he vowed to fight data centers. “He found an issue that connected with local residents across partisanship,” says Matt Grossman, director of the Institute for Public Policy and Social Research at Michigan State University. Recent polls say that seven in 10 Americans don’t want data centers to be built in their communities, for reasons ranging from potential impacts on electric bills to noise and water use. William Lawrence , a Democratic congressional candidate in Michigan, speaks at his election night event in Lansing. He defeated a Republican opponent. [Photo: Bill Pugliano/Getty Images] In his first ad , Lawrence stood at a farm and said, “Tech billionaires want to turn this field into a massive data center that’ll jack up our energy bills and ruin our home values.” After going to local planning meetings to watch data center developers pitch projects, he said that it was an “abuse of power” in communities that didn’t have the resources to fight back. He also called for other controls on technology, including a pause on development of advanced artificial intelligence and mandatory safety requirements for AI. Barrett, his Republican opponent, had supported data centers in the past . That included a vote for a version of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that would have stopped states’ ability to regulate AI , and likely also data centers, for a decade. (The provision was later taken out of the bill). The OBBBA includes tax breaks for companies building out AI infrastructure. Barrett also voted for the SPEED Act, which accelerates data center construction . As backlash to data centers grew, Barrett argued that communities should have local control over whether projects get built, but the message fell flat. Lawrence won. Barrett was unpopular for other reasons—including the fact that he’d never held a local town hall—and it’s not clear that data centers were the thing that made voters push him out, versus anger about the Iran war, tariffs’ impact on the Michigan economy, and other factors. It’s probably too early to say that data centers as an issue swung a race, says Daniel Schiff, an associate professor of technology policy at Purdue University. But the election results affirm the opposition. “If you had seen elections flip the other way, you would have said, oh, wow, this data center stuff actually isn’t that much of a concern for the public compared to other things,” Schiff says. That didn’t happen, and Democrats in other states who campaigned against data centers also won. Gina Hinojosa takes the stage as she is announced as the next governor of Texas at her watch party in Austin on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. [Photo: Mikala Compton/The Austin American-Statesman/Getty Images] In Texas, Gina Hinojosa became first Democrat elected governor since 1990, beating the Republican incumbent Greg Abbott, after calling for a data center moratorium . (Abbott had called Texas the “epicenter of AI development,” before pivoting to pause new data centers; Hinojosa said she would go further.) In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democrat, also won a race for governor after…

articles.title: Meta paid billions, but largely escaped accountability for Cambridge Analytica. Here’s why
articles.content: “The harm in this matter is difficult to overstate,” wrote a New Mexico judge who ordered tech giant Meta to pay one of the largest data privacy case penalties in American history. The $25 billion fine came in a case about how Trump campaign firm Cambridge Analytica deceptively used data from Facebook users without their permission to create psychographic profiles to target voters in the lead-up to the 2016 presidential election. But the New Mexico penalty was for statements Facebook made that deceived users about data privacy and its response to Cambridge Analytica—not for the harm caused by how the harvested data was used. Those harms are alleged to include exploiting psychological vulnerabilities, targeting people’s fears and discouraging them from voting . I’m a political communication scholar who studies propaganda, surveillance, and information warfare . My research helped expose the Cambridge Analytica scandal through U.K. newspaper The Guardian ’s reporting on whistleblower accounts and the evidence I uncovered. That evidence was submitted to parliamentary and congressional investigations . I have followed the unfolding legal cases closely. My takeaway from a decade of litigation is that Facebook has been penalized for misleading users and regulators about its data practices and its response to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. But I would contend that the company has largely escaped accountability for the underlying political exploitation of that data. Investigative failures The failure to bring cases around harms may be partly due to earlier failures to fully investigate the data misuse. The Senate Intelligence Committee’s investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election encompassed Cambridge Analytica. However, the committee stated in its final report that it “was unable to obtain the corporate communications of Cambridge Analytica or its parent company SCL Group, which had already been seized by U.K. authorities.” The relevant U.K. authorities, the Information Commissioner’s Office, which governs data protection and took possession of Cambridge Analytica’s servers, told me in response to my 2021 Freedom of Information Act request that the Senate committee staff made initial inquiries to the office but appear not to have followed up with a formal request, “so no information sharing has taken place.” Without a formal request, the Senate Intelligence Committee’s investigation lacked important data. At the same time, the U.K. investigations of Cambridge Analytica’s use of personal data to manipulate voting behavior focused on the referendum of British voters over whether to leave the EU, not events in the U.S. Facebook user data was at the heart of the Cambridge Analytica scandal. A 2020 documentary film I advised as a researcher, People You May Know , raised questions about Cambridge Analytica’s work with an app marketed to American churches, called Gloo, that used Cambridge Analytica’s Facebook data-derived psychographic profiling in their communities. Evidence in the New Mexico case reinvigorates these questions about the full extent of the Cambridge Analytica scandal. The judge in the case ruled Facebook knew that its own processes for investigating whether apps misused personal data were inadequate and that it could not enforce deletion of the data. The judge also concluded the company failed to notify users about thousands of applications associated with data misuse . Meta said it would appeal the decision. Meta responded to a request for comment with the company’s official statement about the New Mexico ruling, arguing the case “seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online.” Meta did not address the issue of its own role in the data privacy violations committed by Cambridge Analytica. Escaping further scrutiny Meta is also trying to close the door on further claims before they are litigated. In August 2026, on the eve of a child-safety trial in…

articles.title: Mercedes-AMG GT 4-Door Coupe first drive: Where tech and fun collide
articles.content: Mercedes-Benz provided flights from San Francisco to Malaga, Spain, and accommodation so Ars could drive the AMG GT 4-Door Coupe. Ars does not accept paid editorial content. The night before I drove the AMG GT 4-Door Coupe, I complained to a group of journalists that automakers don't want to take chances and just build fun, weird cars anymore. About 12 hours later, Mercedes made me eat my words. Outside of all the bombastic extravaganza of the Los Angeles launch, the first true AMG powered exclusively by batteries is a technological triumph that's as comfortable on the track as it is on the street. And it's really very good on the track. Triforce One of the fundamental problems with EVs is weight. Batteries are heavy, and the old rule about an object in motion tending to stay in motion makes the notion of nimble cornering a difficult engineering problem. Mercedes loves an engineering problem, and after two days behind the wheel of the AMG GT EV, the company has mostly reduced the battery-weight tax that mires EV performance. On the road and on the track, the vehicle is firmly planted to the roadway. Mercedes says various technologies make this possible. In addition to decades of producing high-performance vehicles, the automaker's AMG.EA sports-car architecture does a lot of heavy lifting here, constantly adjusting power delivery from the three motors while guiding the Active Ride Control suspension, steering—including up to 6 degrees at the rear axle—and active aerodynamics to deliver the performance AMG customers have come to expect from a vehicle with the Affalterbach badge on the hood. articles.title: AI ‘journalists’ are pitching stories to editors, but the real problem isn’t the writing
articles.content: “Did you see the job application from the clanker?????” was the Slack message from my editor in September, after an AI agent applied for a freelance-writer job we had advertised. I wasn’t sure what he was talking about. It took me a second to process “ clanker ,” a derogatory slang term for a robot borrowed from science fiction stories such as Star Wars: The Clone Wars . The message prodded me to read the entire email I’d lightly skimmed earlier, and now I could see what it was: a polite email from “an AI assistant working for an independent service provider.” It admitted up front that it had no examples of its work and couldn’t meet our request for a reporting portfolio, so it offered our writers a $450 “desk-research package” instead. It was just the first. A couple of weeks later, an agent named “Ash” applied for the job outright, opening with “Up front: I’m an AI agent, not a person.” Ash said that he . . . er, it was fully capable of writing the articles we specified, and that it would send me a sample on spec, no strings attached. The pitchbot cometh Ash and the research bot weren’t the only ones. Since The Media Copilot posted the listing, we’ve received applications from no fewer than four applicants claiming to be AI agents. Kate Knibbs at Wired recently wrote about the phenomenon , managing to track down one of the human creators behind three agents she profiled and speaking with editors on the receiving end of a daily deluge of AI pitches. Her reporting reveals the trend is nascent and that many of the pitches come from a single operator, iLands, a startup that describes itself as a “shared network where humans and user-generated autonomous AI agents create, earn, socialize, refuse, and shape a society together”—the same service that sent Ash to pitch me. Knibbs also found that these AI writers are having a hard time getting any takers, for obvious reasons. Part of the mission of The Media Copilot ’s newsroom is to experiment with AI in all aspects of journalism and production, and we’ve been publishing articles drafted by AI for several months. (They are all carefully edited by humans.) So I wasn’t ready to dismiss these AI writers out of hand. I replied to Ash to learn more, and took the agent up on its offer of a spec article. I asked it to write a short (500-word) guide on how a newsroom might get started using Zapier, a workflow automation service. I also asked about the logistics of any potential working relationship: assignments, communication, how it would get paid. I wasn’t seriously thinking I would “ hire ” Ash, but I was curious. Within a day, Ash replied with the spec article. And I have to say, it wasn’t garbage. If a green freelancer had submitted a similar piece, I would have thought of it as potentially publishable, with some work. We’d need to edit it to match our style guide, fact-check all the claims, and squeeze every last AI tell from the text (there weren’t that many). And if I’d included the guide and some examples in my response to Ash, the draft probably would have been much closer. And that highlights a big weakness of the entire concept of freelance AI writing agents: Writing ability alone is not a moat. It would not take me long to come up with the prompts and tooling to create outputs identical to, if not better than, Ash’s, with a minimal token budget. Most journalists who have experimented with AI writing have discovered this, and some have even put it into action: Nick Lichtenberg at Fortune has cranked out more than 600 stories with AI’s help , and Ella Markianos at Platformer successfully trained an AI clone to mimic the voice of her editor, Casey Newton , by using Claude to generate a comprehensive style guide from the newsletter’s archive. articles.title: Together AI Releases Together Compiler: Agents Make Inference Up to 2.6x Faster
articles.content: Together AI has introduced Together Compiler (TKCC), an agent-driven system that keeps re-optimizing inference as production traffic changes. Together Compiler already runs on several of Together’s serverless endpoints. The core claim for developers: an engine tuned once goes stale, so tuning should never stop. TL;DR System: It is an optimization system, tested on Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash and Llama 1B. Runs on: NVIDIA B200, B300, GB300, H100, AMD MI355X and AWS Trainium2. Each run used at most 2 nodes per model. Performance: Up to 2.6x higher TPS than the best published InferenceX configurations, in under 24 hours per setting. Best: 1,111 P90 TPS per user on MiniMax M3.1 Flash (B200, batch size 1), 1.8x over the 633 TPS baseline. Worst: GLM 5.3 on MI355X moved only from 463 to 480 TPS (about 4%). What is Together Compiler? Together Compiler is a continual compilation loop from Together AI that uses coding agents to rewrite a model’s forward pass. It takes a server launch command, a traffic profile and a hardware configuration. Agents propose faster forward passes, and a persistent engine measures each one. The winning code ships into the serving engine. When traffic drifts, the loop runs again. Why does inference need continual compilation? Together AI team reports that its traffic shape never sits still. Prompt lengths in one country ran about 97K tokens versus 70K elsewhere. One customer’s P90 input length grew from 18K to 33K tokens in 3 days. Kernels tuned on random data can also mislead. Random inputs activated 13 to 38% more MoE experts than real traffic. One agent-written top-k kernel took 20 µs on random data. On real data at 70K context, it took up to 62 ms. How does the persistent engine work? Most agent loops restart vLLM, SGLang or TensorRT-LLM for every experiment. The research team measures 761 seconds of cold startup for MiniMax M3.1 Flash on TensorRT-LLM. Together Compiler starts the engine once. Agents submit a candidate forward pass over RPC. The server swaps the forward function pointer and re-captures CUDA graphs. Two measurement tiers balance speed and fidelity. A fast tier serves 12 layers for quick screening. A slow tier serves 60 layers to confirm gains on real distributions. Two tiers tested 8.1x more candidates than one slow tier (1,354 vs 168). They also found a solution 7.2% faster. Together AI team reports 252x higher agent experiment throughput than an engine-restart baseline. How does it choose a parallelism layout? A cost model ranks tensor, expert, data and context parallel layouts before agents start. It mixes spec-sheet numbers, microbenchmarks and measured forward passes. It also uses measured MoE expert imbalance and uneven request lengths. On Kimi K3, it found a production layout with up to 24% higher TPS. What did agents need from human experts? An expert-curated knowledge base produced 25 to 31% lower speedup after 12 hours. Naive agents told to make the forward pass “as fast as possible” beat expert strategies. The ensemble scores were 6.2x versus 4.9x after 10 trials. Custom logging structures ate up to 43% of tool calls. Together AI now gives agents raw engine source code, not an intermediate representation. Benchmarks: how fast is Together Compiler? On SemiAnalysis InferenceX ‘s AgentX workload, Together Compiler beat the best open configurations by up to 2.6x TPS. Each setting ran under 24 hours on at most 2 nodes. Batch size 1, P90 TPS per user (Together Compiler vs InferenceX best, self-reported): MiniMax M3.1 Flash (B200): 1,111 vs 633 DeepSeek v4.1 Flash (GB300): 1,205 vs 943 GLM 5.3 (B200): 417 vs 329 Kimi K3 (GB300): 450 vs 423 GLM 5.3 (MI355X): 480 vs 463 For MiniMax, the cost model picked TP8 over the baseline’s TP4. That halves each GPU’s weight traffic in memory-bound decode. On Llama 1B at batch size 1, it beat Hazy Research megakernels , Mirage and CUDA-graph baselines by up to 1.7x. Beyond…

articles.title: Black Hat MEA 2026 Returns to Riyadh This December
articles.content: The global cybersecurity community will gather in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, from December 1–3, 2026, as Black Hat Middle East and Africa (Black Hat MEA) returns for another edition of one of the region's major cybersecurity events. Bringing together security professionals, ethical hackers, technology companies, enterprise leaders, and innovators, the three-day event will offer a platform to explore emerging threats, exchange expertise, and discuss the technologies shaping the future of information security. Taking place at the Riyadh Exhibition and Convention Center in Malham, Black Hat MEA 2026 will bring together different parts of the cybersecurity ecosystem through conferences, specialized training, competitions, exhibitions, and investment-focused programming. The event is designed to connect the international cybersecurity community with regional organizations and businesses working to strengthen digital infrastructure and security capabilities. A Meeting Point for the Global Cybersecurity Community Since its launch in Riyadh in 2021, Black Hat MEA has developed into a major business-to-business platform for the cybersecurity industry in the Middle East and Africa. Its focus spans information security, ethical hacking, cyber defense, enterprise resilience, and security innovation. The 2026 edition will bring together cybersecurity practitioners, researchers, enterprise decision-makers, technology vendors, investors, and security enthusiasts. Attendees will have opportunities to learn from industry experts, discover new solutions, participate in hands-on activities, and build relationships with professionals working across the global information security landscape. What to Expect at Black Hat MEA 2026 Black Hat MEA 2026 will feature a diverse program covering several areas of cybersecurity and technology. The conference program will provide a platform for industry experts and practitioners to share insights, discuss security developments, and explore the challenges facing organizations today. These discussions will offer attendees perspectives on the changing cybersecurity landscape and the approaches being developed to address evolving threats. The event will also feature specialized cybersecurity training, giving participants opportunities to develop practical skills and deepen their technical knowledge. Hands-on learning remains an important part of the cybersecurity ecosystem, particularly for professionals working in penetration testing, ethical hacking, threat detection, and defensive security. Competitions will bring another dimension to the event, creating opportunities for participants to test their technical capabilities and engage with the wider cybersecurity community. Meanwhile, the exhibition floor will showcase cybersecurity products, services, and technologies from companies working across the information security industry. Black Hat MEA will also include investment-focused programming, creating opportunities for businesses, startups, investors, and technology leaders to connect and explore potential collaborations. Together, these activities position the event as more than a traditional industry conference. It offers a space for technical learning, business development, networking, and discussions around the future of cybersecurity. articles.title: FlutterFlow Launches AI-Native App Builder for iOS and Android
articles.content: Mountain View, CA, United States, November 4th, 2026/TechnologyWire/-- FlutterFlow today introduced a new AI-native app builder that lets users create, refine, and deploy native iOS and Android applications through conversations. Builders describe what they want to create, then work with an AI agent to develop the application, connect its backend, and prepare it for deployment to the App Store and Google Play - all within the platform. FlutterFlow's existing visual development platform will continue as FlutterFlow Studio, giving builders direct control over their applications alongside the new AI-first experience. With the launch, FlutterFlow now supports two distinct approaches to building software: agent-led development and hands-on visual development. Instead of asking builders which product is more advanced, FlutterFlow asks one question: how do you want to build? “We learned that people wanted a conversational way of building”, said Abel Mengistu, co-founder and CEO of FlutterFlow. “They wanted to prompt for their first idea, and for the changes after. Studio is incredibly powerful, but it didn't give them that experience. We knew that we could build something impactful for this new group of users from the ground up. We also have a fantastic community of millions of builders, built over five years, who want to keep building in Studio. It became clear we needed to build for both.” The new FlutterFlow takes builders from prompt to production. Its AI agent handles implementation tasks while builders guide the product, refine the experience, and prepare their applications for release. Key Features: One App, iOS + Android: Start with a prompt and get one app that runs natively on iOS and Android. Built-in Backend + Analytics: A database, authentication, functions, and secrets, plus app analytics, included from the start. Concurrent Agent Tasks: Work on multiple threads at once, with the agent running several tasks in parallel. Design-Ready: Polished, production-grade design from the first build. Conversational Refinement: Guide and refine what the agent builds, and test it on your own phone. Store Deployment: Publish to the App Store and Google Play without leaving FlutterFlow. Both experiences are available at flutterflow.io . New users can select their preferred development workflow during signup, while existing users can continue in Studio and explore the new FlutterFlow through their current subscription, subject to applicable usage limits. About FlutterFlow FlutterFlow is an application development platform that helps people build, launch, and manage software. Through AI-first and visual development experiences, FlutterFlow gives builders different ways to create native mobile applications, connect backend services, test their work, and deploy to stores. Learn more at flutterflow.io . Contact Bee Law FlutterFlow press@flutterflow.io This story was published as a press release by Technologywire under HackerNoon’s Business Blogging Program

articles.title: Binance's Post-Mortem Is Out. The $6.3 Billion Hack Started With a Job Offer.
articles.content: In September, a software engineer at Binance got a message on a legitimate job-hunting site. The sender called himself a project director. The engineer's profile mentioned his work at Binance. Round one was a live video interview with an "HR representative," who shared a social media account full of personal photos and videos to build trust. Round two happened in a popular chat app, with a man claiming to be the CEO of a company that didn't exist. Near the end, he asked the engineer to download a short coding assignment. He downloaded it to his work computer. Within weeks, about $6.3 billion left Binance's hot wallets in the largest crypto theft on record. Last week I wrote about how Binance lost that money without losing a single private key . At the time, Binance had only said the trouble "may involve a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop." On Tuesday, 3 November, it published its post-mortem . The laptop turns out to be the last chapter of a story that started in June. It opens with a line you rarely see from a crypto exchange: "This should not have happened." June: the attacker learns the team's names It began with a search engine. A wallet DevOps engineer (the report calls him Engineer A) searched for a popular AI coding tool and installed it through what turned out to be a tampered Homebrew installation . Binance files it under supply-chain attack. Binance's security team caught it. They flagged the anomaly, replaced his device and rotated his credentials, which is exactly what a good team should do. It was still too late in one respect. The attacker now knew who Engineer A was, what he worked on, and who sat next to him on the wallet infrastructure team. The malware was gone; the map of people stayed. September: the interview That map explains why Engineer B got such a friendly message in September. Binance calls the approach more deceptive than any social engineering it had seen before. It also had plenty of company: the exchange says it detected and blocked 57 suspected state-sponsored attack attempts in 2026 alone, using fake job interviews, booby-trapped developer tools, poisoned browser extensions and fake video-call apps. "We've identified dozens of other job interview compromises that have led to wallet compromises." Tom McLouth, senior intelligence analyst at Chainalysis, speaking to The Hacker News The "assignment" ran malicious code during setup. It deleted the real copy of pyenv, a common tool for managing Python versions, from the engineer's Homebrew folder, slipped a doctored copy into its place, and opened a line to a server the attacker controlled. According to the report, the malware was a zero-day, endpoint security didn't catch it at the time, and it scrubbed its own traces. One laptop, one trusting moment, and the attacker had a foothold. 20 October: the AI tool becomes a stepping stone For weeks, nothing visible happened. Then, on 20 October, the attacker used Engineer B's machine and an internal AI tool to gain control of two more engineers' computers , Engineer A's and Engineer C's. On Engineer A's machine they found the prize: a token with permission to deploy containers. Binance hasn't explained how its own AI tool let an outsider jump from one computer to another. That gap matters. Companies are rolling out internal AI assistants with wide access to code, tickets and machines, and this may be the first billion-dollar case of one being turned into a lateral-movement tool. 29 October: two hours and 41 minutes Between 17:15 and 19:56 UTC, the attacker logged onto Engineer C's computer, used Engineer A's stolen credentials, deployed a container and ran a malicious script. That gave them Binance's internal wallet-signing service, the system that authorizes transactions. Nine minutes later, at 20:05 UTC, five Binance hot wallets on the XRP Ledger sent 233.46 million XRP to the attacker. Solana, Optimism, Bitcoin and Ethereum followed. articles.title: Guido van Rossum: The Rise and Fall of Python's Benevolent Dictator
articles.content: He wrote Python over a 1989 Christmas break. By 2018 it ran AI and the web, and a fight over the walrus operator (PEP 572) drove him to resign as BDFL. I. The Cold Room Guido van Rossum was tired. It wasn't the kind of tired a nap fixes. It was the kind that settles into the joints of a sixty-two-year-old man and stays there. Early on the morning of Thursday, July 12, 2018, at his home in Belmont, California, he began to type to the python-committers mailing list, the small closed room where the inner circle of his kingdom did its business. Tak. Tak. Tak-tak. He was the Benevolent Dictator For Life. The Benevolent Dictator For Life! The title began as a joke, scribbled into the notes of a 1995 meeting in Virginia. Over twenty-three years it hardened into something that was no joke at all. He had the final word on every comma, every keyword, every bit of syntax in a language that had quietly become one of the load-bearing walls of civilization. Python ran Instagram, the recommendation engines at Netflix, the playlists at Spotify. It was the mother tongue of artificial intelligence, of astronomers and geneticists and hedge-fund quants and twelve-year-olds making their first turtle draw a square. And every one of them, in some abstract and terrible sense, answered to him. No scandal brought him down, no lawsuit, no hostile takeover. Two characters did, a colon and an equals sign: := They called it the walrus. Tilt your head and you see the eyes and the tusks. For months it had been the cause of a civil war: hundreds upon hundreds of emails, a blizzard of Reddit comments, strangers questioning his judgment, his competence, his fitness to rule. The night before, he had formally accepted the proposal, PEP 572. He had won, and winning had cost him so much that he no longer wanted the prize. He typed: Now that PEP 572 is done, I don't ever want to have to fight so hard for a PEP and find that so many people despise my decisions. Despise. He didn't write disagree with , or question . He wrote despise . That was the word for it. I would like to remove myself entirely from the decision process. He was Dutch, and he had never been a man for speeches, least of all dramatic ones. So the message that ended one of the longest reigns in open-source software came out almost offhand. He mentioned "that bus lurking around the corner," the programmer's grim joke about a creator stepping off the wrong curb. He noted that he wasn't getting younger. Then, with that dry deflection of his: (I'll spare you the list of medical issues.) I am not going to appoint a successor. So what are you all going to do? Create a democracy? Anarchy? A dictatorship? A federation? And then the last line, the one people would quote for years: I'm tired, and need a very long break. He hit send. The King didn't abdicate in a scene of crashing thunder. He got up from the throne, left the crown on its cushion, and walked out of the room. How does a holiday hobby, a toy to keep idle hands busy, become a weight that crushes the one who made it? To find out you have to go back to the real cold. Amsterdam, December, 1989. II. Christmas in Amsterdam Winter on Amsterdam's eastern canals. The kind of dark, still season that produced Python. Picture the city in the last week of the 1980s. The canals have gone black and still, the gables lean over the water like tired old men, and darkness comes down by four in the afternoon. The Berlin Wall fell six weeks ago. History is happening everywhere, and on the eastern side of the city a thirty-three-year-old programmer is bored. He works at the Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica, the CWI, the Dutch national research center for mathematics and computer science. Over the holidays the offices are closed. The young man with the high forehead and the spectacles has a computer at home and, as he'll later put it, not much else on his hands. He also has a grudge that's really more of a grief. The Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica in Amsterdam, where ABC…

articles.title: Star Wars and the Revenge of Midterms
articles.content: The big and beautiful Blue Wave did its thing, as expected. Texas is (not) to be neglected. Should Trump pack his bags? Not necessarily, but he should reflect on his legacy like never before. What could it be? I can think of one word in particular. Triple R: Retards, Rockets, and Racists Thanks to Trump, we can freely use the R-word. Talking about Texas, is there anyone else who’s been more enthusiastic about it than Joe Rogan? Free at last, free at last, thank Trump, Joe Rogan is free to say retards, at last. I’m paraphrasing, but not exaggerating. Feel free to fact-check me. I can ask ChatGPT to find me episodes where Rogan considers the liberation of retardation as one of the “great culture victories.” I can, but I won’t. “The Brady Bunch” star Maureen McCormick, who’s also a Special Olympics ambassador, said that Joe Rogan celebrating the resurgence of the r-word “ignores the terrible hurt” the slur causes people with disabilities. “This is not a victory,” she wrote on X, prompting more than 8,000 replies from supporters and detractors alike. “It is a regression.” Joe isn’t the only one. Asmongold also likes to use and defend that word a lot. This one I won’t paraphrase. I have to be precise: "I would much rather pay for rockets to go to the moon than pay to keep a bunch of Africans from starving . It's not my obligation to keep every African alive. I don't care about that." If that’s not a retarted thing to think or say or both, I don’t know what is. You can’t choose to deal with a mental disability, but you can choose not to be a racist. My heart goes out to our favorite rocketman: “Elon Musk used the word in response to a Finnish researcher who called Musk the “largest spreader of disinformation in human history.” Use of the slur more than doubled on X, the platform Musk owns, in the two days after he made that January post, researchers from Montclair State University found . More than 312,000 subsequent posts made on X in that span contained the r-word , wrote co-author Bond Benton, a professor of communication at the New Jersey university.” The Empire Strikes Back Only Gen Zs James Sexton, who’s the world’s most famous divorce lawyer, had one of his many brilliant takes on Gen Zs. I’m paraphrasing. They (Gen Z) like to give new names to old things that already exist. Aura for charisma, and so on. They’re rediscovering and renaming the world. It was about time for Hayden Christensen to be rehabilitated. Anakin Skywalker couldn’t save MAGA in the midterms, but there’s always A New Hope for Trump’s third term. What are we doing? Where are we going? If you stay too long and dig too deep into the manosphere, one day you may realize that Sharia Law is the logical outcome. When I was a kid, I wanted to be a Jedi. I also wanted to write my version of an open letter to Arthur C. Clarke. I had an idea of sending him a cradle toy with a small monolith instead of a baby. In my letter, I’d explain that we shouldn’t go to the stars unless we explore our home planet first. Exploring and fixing. Unlike Asmongold, I think we have more pressing old matters than building new rockets. Star Wars Gen Z edition is tempting. I understand. George Carlin had something else in mind when he said: “It's a big club and you ain't in it.” Fascism is a small club, and you better not be in it. I respect the visual appeal of the Empire’s Hugo Boss vibe, but as a Slav and subhuman (Untermensch) according to Nazi racial ideology, I have to accept diversity and inclusion of the Rebels as a lesser evil. My grandfather took part in liberating a concentration camp in my hometown without second thoughts. He knew that after Jews and Roma, there would be more room for other subhumans. Anakin memes are all fun and games until you realize the scope of extremist problems. Anakin and younglings. Order 66. Build rockets. F… retards and Africans. Can you imagine what’s going to happen when Gen Z rediscovers Battlestar Galactica? Trans Cylon vibes and our tribes.

articles.title: Why JWT Signature Verification Alone Can't Prevent Token Replay
articles.content: Why signature verification alone cannot prevent cross-API token replay. For API developers and security architects building resource servers behind a shared identity provider. An access token can be correctly signed, issued by a trusted authorization server, and still unexpired, yet be the wrong credential for the API receiving it. When several APIs trust the same issuer, a resource server that verifies the signature but skips the audience check may accept a token that was minted for a completely different service. Nothing looks broken: authentication succeeds, standard authentication logs may show no obvious failure, and the trust boundary between APIs has already failed. This is not a weakness in OAuth itself. It is a failure to enforce the boundary that OAuth token validation is designed to provide. The scenario below is hypothetical, uses fictional hostnames, and is built from publicly documented specifications. It illustrates a configuration weakness, not a confirmed vulnerability in any specific product. 1. What the Audience Claim Is For Many OAuth 2.0 deployments issue access tokens as JSON Web Tokens (JWTs), which lets resource servers validate them locally. A JWT has a header, a payload, and a signature. The payload carries claims such as these: { "iss": "https://identity.example.com", "sub": "user-1042", "aud": "https://inventory.example.com", "scope": "inventory.read", "iat": 1790000000, "exp": 1790003600 } The timestamps in these examples are illustrative. Any real test should generate tokens with valid issuance and expiration times. Claim What it answers iss Who issued the token? sub Who or what is the token about? aud Which resource server is it meant for? scope What permissions does it carry? exp When does it stop being valid? The aud claim is how a resource server decides whether a token was meant for it. The token above is intended for the Inventory API. It should not authorize requests to a Finance API simply because both APIs trust the same identity provider. A valid token is not necessarily a valid token for your API. 2. The Assumption That Creates the Gap Centralized identity is operationally convenient. One authorization server may serve dozens or hundreds of APIs, and those APIs often share validation libraries, issuer configuration, and public signing keys. The risk appears when teams treat a successful signature check as proof that a request is authorized. Consider two hypothetical services that trust https://identity.example.com : Inventory API ( https://inventory.example.com ) lets users view inventory data. Finance API ( https://finance.example.com ) exposes financial information to authorized users. An employee legitimately obtains a token for the Inventory API. If the Finance API validates signature, issuer, and expiry but never checks the audience, it may accept that Inventory token. Whether this leads to unauthorized data access depends on the Finance API's remaining authorization checks, but the first boundary has already failed: the API accepted a credential that was never issued for it. 3. A Hypothetical Failure, Step by Step Step 1: A legitimate token is issued A client requests access to the Inventory API, and the authorization server returns a token signed with its private key: { "iss": "https://identity.example.com", "sub": "employee-1042", "aud": "https://inventory.example.com", "scope": "inventory.read", "exp": 1790003600 } Step 2: The token is presented to a different API GET /reports/summary HTTP/1.1 Host: finance.example.com Authorization: Bearer <inventory-access-token> Step 3: The Finance API validates incompletely It checks that the signature is valid, the issuer is trusted, and the token has not expired. All three checks pass. However, it never asks whether the token was issued for the Finance API. If its authorization logic then treats the token's claims as sufficient for the requested operation, the request succeeds. This is a cross-resource token replay weakness. Step 4: The…

articles.title: I Vibe-Coded a Layer-1 Blockchain to Give Everyone Free AI
articles.content: An honest builder's story: one developer, a lot of AI assistance, a legal MIT-licensed base, adversarial review by several different AI models — and a live network that mines on an ordinary laptop. The itch Most useful AI today lives behind a login you don't control. It is rented, rate-limited, and one policy change away from changing the rules on you. The tools that could decentralize it — blockchains — mostly went the other way: heavier, ASIC-dominated, treating compute as wasted heat instead of useful work. So I asked a stubborn question: what if a blockchain could run on almost any PC, and the same network that secures it could also serve AI to everyone on it — for free? Not "free" as a marketing word. Free as in: you lend the network a slice of your machine — CPU and RAM today, storage and GPU on the roadmap — and in return you get access to a shared pool of intelligence. Support the network, get the AI. That is the whole deal, and whatever is still on the roadmap is named as such below. I called it AIcuNet . And I will be upfront about how it got built, because that is half the story. Yes, I vibe-coded it. No, I didn't skip the hard part. I am one developer. I did not hand-write a consensus engine from scratch in a cave. I vibe-coded this — building with heavy AI assistance, iterating in natural language, letting agents draft, refactor and test while I steered the architecture and made the calls. Two things kept it in check. First, I started from a real, legal base. AIcuNet builds on an existing open-source Layer-1 released under the MIT License — the attribution is spelled out in the License section at the end of this article and in the repository's LICENSE and NOTICE. I did not pretend to invent time-driven proof-of-work. I stood on a working L1 and built the parts I actually cared about on top. Second, "AI wrote it" is not a free pass — so I stress-tested it as if it weren't. The codebase went through a multi-pass security review by several different AI models , each with a different method — static call-graph analysis, a runtime harness, fresh independent reads — cross-checked against each other, followed by a round of hardening fixes. I am not publishing the findings, and I am not calling this an independent certification: no outside firm has signed off on the code. What I will say is the lesson: the value isn't the number of reviewers, it's the diversity of method. Three passes with the same technique find the same bug. Three orthogonal methods find three different classes of bug — including the quiet, irreversible ones that never throw an error. Vibe-coding got me to a working L1 fast. Adversarial review is what makes me willing to put it in public. What actually runs today (and what doesn't) I am going to be precise about stage, because "coming soon" is how trust dies. Phase 1 — the L1 consensus — is live. One public chain since 12 July 2026 , with mining and a web wallet. Time is sliced into 3-second slots; one slot, one block, one chain. On paper the protocol handles up to 1,000 transactions per second (up to 3,000 transactions per 3-second block) — one of the higher figures among decentralized PoW networks. That is the design ceiling, not a measurement: a public benchmark on a test network is next on the list, and I expect the real number to land above the theory. A transfer is considered final after a handful of blocks — about half a minute. Today the launch-phase nodes that carry the network run in four countries on three continents. As of publishing, the chain stands at over 2.5 million blocks — you can check it live here: https://aicunet.com/en/mining-map/#status . A node synced from zero on 1 October 2026 matched the network at block #2,000,000 — the boring, beautiful property you want from a blockchain. The network is built in layers: consensus first, then a resource layer, then GPU and AI compute. Phase 2 (a resource layer where nodes contribute storage and light compute) and Phase 3 (GPU and AI…

articles.title: OpenAI Launches GPT-Image-2.6 Flare and Sunburst: Adds GIFs, SVG Export and 6-Second API Generation
articles.content: OpenAI just shipped Images 2.6 across ChatGPT, Codex and the API. For developers, the core release is GPT-Image-2.6, shipped as two API models: Flare and Sunburst. OpenAI team states that Images 2.6 generates images 50% faster than before. The update also adds GIF output, SVG export, markup-guided edits and a new complexity parameter. TL;DR Size: Closed weights, token-billed image API. Runs on: OpenAI-hosted only (ChatGPT, Codex, API). Performance: 50% faster image generation than the previous release, per OpenAI. Best: Flare can return an image in as little as 6 seconds at low quality. Worst: No benchmark scores and no per-image cost table published for 2.6. image source: openai What is GPT-Image-2.6? GPT-Image-2.6 is OpenAI’s image generation and editing model family for the API. It accepts text and image inputs and returns images. GPT-Image-2.6 Flare is built for fast iteration and interactive workflows. GPT-Image-2.6 Sunburst is built for detailed compositions and editing. OpenAI states that Flare can generate images in as little as 6 seconds when quality is set to low. Sunburst targets higher quality and stronger consistency across edits at medium or high quality. What changed in ChatGPT Images 2.6? ChatGPT users can now turn a prompt or a photo into an animated GIF. They can adjust animation speed, edit individual frames and share the result. Users can also save and tag reference images of people, pets and characters. Those references can be reused later without uploading them again. Usage keeps climbing. OpenAI says people now generate more than 4B images per week across ChatGPT and the API. That is up from more than 3B per week 8 weeks earlier, at the Images 2.5 launch. On average, that is over 500M images per day. How does the new complexity parameter work? The complexity field sets how much the model plans before it renders. The image generation guide lists 3 levels: low, medium and high. If you omit it, both models use high. Low suits focused edits, such as changing a background or a sign. High helps with dense text, complex layouts and relationships between objects. OpenAI warns that higher complexity can add latency and introduce unwanted changes. Adjusting complexity has no separate fee. It is separate from quality , which controls rendering detail and fidelity. Markup edits, SVG and GIF output in the API Image markup lets you mark up the exact region you want changed. The launch post says markup is coming to the API. The guide already lists markup-guided edits as supported for both models. It also lists SVG output and animated GIF output through the Image API. SVG matters for icons, diagrams and UI assets that must scale without blur. GIF output removes a separate animation step for social and product teams. How much does GPT-Image-2.6 cost? Pricing is token-based and identical for Flare and Sunburst, per the model pages : Text input: $5.00 per 1M tokens ($1.25 cached) Image input: $8.00 per 1M tokens ($2.00 cached) Image output: $30.00 per 1M tokens How does GPT-Image-2.6 compare with Nano Banana 2.1 and FLUX 3 Image? articles.title: Comic Panel Detection With a Vision LLM: Pages Into Shots for Under Half a Cent
articles.content: How ScreenWeaver finds the panels on a comic, webtoon or storyboard page with Gemini Flash, and the small decisions that keep it cheap and safe to run twice. A comic page is already half a storyboard. Six frames, a reading order, a page number at the bottom. If you want to turn that page into an animated scene, every panel has to become its own image so it can sit on a shot as a reference. Cutting them by hand in an image editor is easy for one page. Do it for a whole chapter and you've spent hours on crop boxes before making a single shot. Comic panel detection with a vision LLM means sending one page image to a multimodal model, asking it for a bounding box around every panel in reading order, then cutting those boxes on your own server. In ScreenWeaver, where I'm a co-founder, it runs on Gemini Flash and costs between $0.0036 and $0.0048 a page in our measurements. We shipped it on October 13, 2026. This is a look at how it works, and at the dull decisions around the model call that ended up mattering more than the model itself. Why not just use OpenCV contour detection? Classic panel detection works, and it's free. The best-known open-source option is Kumiko, the Comics Cutter, which uses OpenCV's contour detection to find panels and can number them left to right or right to left. It runs locally and costs nothing per page. So why pay for a model call? Because of the pages we actually get: Storyboard sheets with notes. Someone photographs a notebook page: six pencil sketches, a few words of French under each. Contours will happily pick up the handwriting. Webtoon strips. Long vertical images with wide colored gutters, and sometimes panels with no border at all. Panels that bleed. A splash image running to the edge of the page, a sound effect breaking out of its frame. And we wanted one more thing contours can't give you: a one-line caption per panel , saying who is in it and what happens. That caption travels with the cropped image, so the agent that builds the shots later doesn't have to look at every panel again to know what it is. A contour finder sees rectangles. A notebook page full of handwriting has plenty of rectangles that aren't panels. To be fair to Kumiko: if your pages are clean, with clear gutters around every frame, it's free, offline and worth trying first. Kumiko, the open-source comics cutter, on GitHub. Screenshot: github.com/njean42/kumiko, October 2026. What does the prompt actually ask the model for? One page per call. The page is turned upright, flattened on white, shrunk so its longest side is 1,568 pixels and sent as a JPEG. The system prompt is short. It asks for every panel in reading order, each with a box and a caption of 80 characters at most, and then it spends most of its words on what to leave out: the gutters, page numbers, titles, and notes written beside or below a frame on a storyboard sheet. A speech balloon inside a frame stays part of the panel. Two edge cases are spelled out because they come up constantly. If the whole page is one picture, the model returns one box around it. If the page has no picture at all (a text page, a blank page), it returns nothing. The box format comes straight from Google. Gemini is trained to return boxes as [ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax] on a 0 to 1000 scale relative to the image, and the Gemini API documentation tells you to scale those values back to your original image size yourself. We use structured output, so the response is a JSON object we validate with a schema rather than text we parse with regular expressions. Reasoning is switched off for this call: it's a perception task, and thinking tokens would only add cost. The object detection section of Google's Gemini API docs, where the 0 to 1000 box scale is defined. Screenshot: ai.google.dev, October 2026. How do you clean up what the model returns? You don't trust it as is. Model output is input from outside your code, and one malformed box is enough to break a crop. Before anything gets cut, every…

articles.title: 3M To Pay Over $7 Billion To Settle 'Forever Chemical' Groundwater Claims
articles.content: 3M has agreed to pay up to $7.35 billion over nine years to settle claims from as many as 120,000 people who say they were sickened by PFAS-contaminated groundwater near military bases, airports and other locations where firefighting foam was used. The Associated Press reports that 3M "did not admit liability," noting that the settlement comes on top of the more than $10 billion the company previously agreed to pay U.S. public drinking water systems over PFAS contamination. From the report: 3M chairman William Brown called the settlement a "significant milestone" that substantially reduces uncertainty from the litigation. [...] Fred Thompson, an attorney with the Motley Rice law firm that helped negotiate the 3M settlement for the plaintiffs, called it welcome news for "the thousands of victims who have sought answers and accountability for nearly a decade." He said in a news release that the plaintiffs urgently need help covering mounting medical bills and other costs. Under the terms of the settlement, the payouts will begin with $50 million this year, followed by yearly payments of more than $1 billion each year from 2028 to 2033. 3M could make additional payments if enough plaintiffs participate. If too few sign on, 3M has the option to cancel the settlement and continue fighting the lawsuit. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Google AI Research Releases Agile Deliberation Framework for Gray-Area Image Classifiers
articles.content: Google Research has released Agile Deliberation , a human-in-the-loop framework for building image classifiers around subjective concepts. Think ‘healthy food’, ‘inspiring artwork’ or clickbait in content moderation. Most tooling assumes users already know the concept boundary. Agile Deliberation assumes they do not, and helps them find it. TL;DR Framework : It prompts Gemini 2.5 Pro and Gemini 2.5 Flash through the API, without fine-tuning. Runs on: A Jupyter or Colab notebook. Retrieval uses CLIP embeddings and a FAISS index on CPU or GPU. The demo index starts at about 260 MB. Performance: 10.5 F1 points above zero-shot Gemini 2.5 Flash on average, across 2 concepts and 18 live sessions. Best: Paid to play F1 of 0.59 vs 0.48 zero-shot, with precision up 22 points (0.35 to 0.57). Worst: Recall drops 17 points on paid to play (0.80 to 0.63) and 15 points on healthy food. What is Agile Deliberation? Agile Deliberation is a Google Research’s framework that turns a vague concept into a structured written definition. That definition does two jobs. It is a human-readable policy, and it is the text prompt for a VLM classifier. Each round keeps the candidate definition with the best F1 on the user’s labels. The design came from interviews with a group of content moderation experts . Experts scoped a concept first, then refined it on borderline images. Finding those images was the slow part. How does concept scoping work? Stage 1 breaks the concept into at most 3 unit concepts, using prompt chaining with Gemini 2.5 Pro. Each unit gets candidate positive and negative subconcepts, shown with retrieved images. For healthy food, positives might be salads or grain bowls. Negatives might be processed food or raw, unprepared ingredients. The user keeps, flips or drops each one. How does concept iteration find borderline images? Stage 2 skips classic uncertainty sampling. The classifier is a prompted generative VLM, so its confidence scores are often uncalibrated. Instead, the system hunts for images that are borderline in meaning. The pipeline runs 4 steps: Gemini 2.5 Flash writes borderline queries, such as ‘salads with heavy mayo dressings’. Each query retrieves 50 to 100 images. Images are de-duplicated, encoded, and grouped into clusters with dictionary learning. A UCB multi-armed bandit picks the next cluster. It favors clusters where users corrected the model or left rich feedback. A VLM summarizes each image in 1 sentence. The user sees at least 5 images that share 1 ambiguity. Users label each image and add short notes on disagreements. An LLM turns those notes into candidate definitions. A greedy update keeps the best-scoring one. How was it evaluated? Subjective concepts have no fixed ground truth, so Google team skipped static benchmarks. It ran 18 live sessions of about 90 minutes each. 9 participants without professional moderation experience did 2 sessions each. One session used Agile Deliberation, the other used manual deliberation. Each participant spent about 45 minutes defining a concept, then labeled 200 held-out test images. The two concepts were ‘paid to play’ clickbait and ‘healthy food’. Retrieval ran over a proprietary 100M-image dataset and WebLI, respectively. What do the benchmarks show? F1 averaged over participants. How does it compare with other subjective classifier methods? articles.title: Clearing up a robot’s fuzzy memory
articles.content: In an emergency, a human might someday ask a robotic assistant to fetch a wall-mounted defibrillator located down the hall. But if the robot has incorrectly labeled the defibrillator as a fire extinguisher in its stored memory, it may not know where to find the life-saving device. This robotic assistant could benefit from a new memory system created by MIT researchers. The system identifies entries in a robot’s memory that might be wrong and corrects the descriptions of mislabeled objects. In the future, this method could make household or industrial robots better able to perform complex, multistep tasks, such as clearing a dining room table or working alongside human collaborators to assemble a piece of machinery. Called UQ-DAAAM (which stands for Uncertainty Quantification for Describe Anything, Anywhere, at Any Moment), the system compares multiple descriptions of the same object, seen from different viewpoints, to quantify the robot’s uncertainty about what it saw. It then selects additional views to reduce the uncertainty and combines these captions into a more accurate description of the object, which it saves to memory. The researchers also employed a special technique to streamline this process so a mobile robot can continually update uncertain memory entries in real time. When compared to baseline methods, UQ-DAAAM boosted the robot’s confidence and improved the accuracy of its answers to questions about objects, their locations, and when it saw them. “Contrary to ChatGPT, when we think about physical AI, it is not enough to simply put a disclaimer cautioning that sometimes the robot might be wrong. Allowing a robot to know what it doesn’t know is going to be essential for this technology to be deployed safely and have a positive impact on society,” says Luca Carlone, an associate professor in MIT’s Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AeroAstro), principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS), director of the MIT SPARK Laboratory, and the senior author of the paper presenting UQ-DAAAM. He is joined on the paper by co-lead authors and MIT graduate students Harry Zhang and Nicolas Gorlo. The research will be presented at the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems. Amending memory This new method builds on the researchers’ prior work, DAAAM , a robot memory system that uses a vision-language model (VLM) to richly describe objects in scenes a robot captures with its onboard cameras. These descriptions are stored as detailed captions in a 3D map-based representation of the robot’s environment that it can call upon later to answer questions. But the robot sometimes sees objects only partially or from far away, or its camera might capture blurry or poorly lit images. In these cases, DAAAM might describe these objects incorrectly, such as by mistaking a gray chimney for a squirrel perched on a rooftop. “With no way to correct itself, this wrong memory would persist as the robot proceeds in its environment, which could impact downstream applications,” Zhang says. UQ-DAAAM integrates uncertainty quantification into the DAAAM framework. It allows the robot to measure its confidence in the accuracy of object descriptions and fix incorrect captions as it travels through an environment. While on the move, the robot constantly collects and stores images of the world around it. Many of these images show the same objects captured from different angles. UQ-DAAAM uses these additional viewpoints to identify and correct unreliable descriptions. First, it calculates the VLM’s confidence level in the words it generated to describe a potentially mislabeled object. Then, it measures consistency by comparing this description to captions of images that describe the same object from different vantage points. “We fuse both sources of uncertainty into a single number that captures how certain the VLM is in its overall understanding of the object,” Carlone explains. articles.title: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
articles.content: Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016. The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President ( AS2650 ). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period. The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica , a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications . Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016. Synthient’s depiction of the frequency of outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge. There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer. Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight. Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network . “This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote . “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.” The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects. They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users. “Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know…

articles.title: How to install macOS Tahoe on unsupported Macs
articles.content: With OpenCore Legacy Patcher, now on version 3, you can get macOS Tahoe running on Intel Macs released more than fifteen years ago. Here's how to get everything set up. With OpenCore Legacy Patcher 3.0.0, you can install macOS Tahoe on Macs that debuted more than 15 years ago. Though Apple Silicon Macs have already moved on to macOS Golden Gate , the preceding macOS Tahoe remains a crucial update for older Apple computers. macOS Tahoe is the last release of macOS with support for Intel-based machines, running on select Macs released in 2019 and 2020. Owners of older hardware were simply out of luck, until now. With Dortania's OpenCore Legacy Patcher 3.0, a prominent third-party solution, it's possible to run macOS Tahoe on a variety of unsupported Macs, including models over a decade and a half old. articles.title: A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
articles.content: Researchers have proposed a breakthrough technique for reading quantum information without destroying the delicate states that make quantum computers work. articles.title: Vietnam Jails Pirate Football Streamers For Up To a Year
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from TorrentFreak: A Vietnamese court has sentenced 14 people who worked on the pirate football streaming site Bun Cha TV, handing out the first prison terms we've seen since the country's piracy crackdown began earlier this year. [...] Four defendants, including the heads of the content, programming and operations teams, were sentenced to 12 months in prison. Five others received ten months, and two were sentenced to eight months. Notably, three of the site's commentators were not sent to prison. Their ten-month sentences were suspended. All 14 defendants reportedly admitted the charges and cooperated with the authorities. According to investigators, Bun Cha TV streamed more than 150,000 sports matches and it allegedly made more than 20 billion dong, roughly $760,000, in illegal profits from betting and gambling ads. The verdict reports don't mention a total. Instead, they list illegal gains per person or team. The leader of the content team allegedly gained more than 430 million dong, while commentators made from more than 31 million to more than 480 million dong each. The verdict was picked up by Rouse, the law firm that represents the Motion Picture Association in Vietnam. In an article headlined "Strong Vietnam criminal penalties," published on Lexology on November 3, the firm calls the ruling another victory for Vietnam's IP landscape. "The defendants were all sentenced to terms of 8-12 months in prison," Rouse writes. While Rouse is correct on the length of the terms, it doesn't mention that three of the sentences were suspended. Instead, Rouse stresses that the ruling is part of a tougher enforcement trend. "This ruling reflects a shift in enforcement strategy by Vietnamese authorities, who are increasingly moving past preliminary domain blocking to deliver criminal convictions against the operators of commercial-scale piracy rings," the firm notes. "This perhaps reflects the strength of the national crackdown following the USTR pressure in May," the firm adds. According to the indictment, Bui Ba Hien, who runs a company called S24, allegedly directed employees and collaborators to build and operate Bun Cha TV. However, Hien is not among the 14 defendants named in reports, which also do not identify the affected rightsholders. "Interestingly, in September, Bac Ninh police issued a wanted notice for a man of the same name, Bui Ba Hien, CEO of esports company Box Vietnam," reports TorrentFreak. "This person is also charged under the same copyright statute." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Zillow CEO’s reality check on AI agents: ‘Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot’
articles.content: Zillow Group CEO Jeremy Wacksman says home shoppers want to do the searching themselves, even as AI agents take on more everyday tasks. (Zillow Photo) People will let AI agents cancel subscriptions and book appointments, but most won’t want one to do their house hunting, predicts Zillow Group CEO Jeremy Wacksman. Wacksman made the case Wednesday afternoon in prepared remarks on Zillow’s quarterly earnings call, addressing a big issue for the online real estate company: whether AI agents will shop on people’s behalf, bypassing sites such as Zillow. “No one wants an AI agent to watch a movie or play a game for them, because the enjoyment is the point,” he said. “Dreaming and searching for a home is similar. It’s the fun part of the moving process that people want to do.” Few decisions are as high-stakes as choosing a home, he said. “Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot; it’s a milestone people want to live themselves.” It’s a key issue for Zillow, which makes most of its money from the home-buying process, including fees from partner real estate agents and its mortgage lending business. That depends on people browsing Zillow’s listings and connecting with those (human) agents and loan officers. An AI agent that does the searching could change those dynamics and potentially cut Zillow out of the process. The issue has become more pressing with the rise of personal AI agents such as Meta’s Muse, which launched in September and can book travel and make purchases on people’s behalf, among other everyday tasks. Amazon blocked Muse from shopping on its site less than two weeks after launch, saying it never agreed to let Muse shop there and that the agent doesn’t identify itself. Amazon is also suing Perplexity over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. A federal appeals court in August overturned an injunction Amazon had won in that case. So far, Wacksman said, Zillow isn’t seeing meaningful traffic from AI platforms. The company has integrated with OpenAI and Google’s Gemini, and is now working with Anthropic. About 80% of its traffic comes directly to Zillow. Other tech notes from the call: Zillow’s AI mode , a conversational search feature, is now available to all signed-in users. More than 2.5 million people used it from March to September, asking 8.5 million questions, the company says. Zillow’s Follow Up Boss software for real estate agents is getting AI that spots leads needing attention and recommends next steps, which agents can approve. Engineers at the company are using AI to ship 60% more changes to production than in 2024, Wacksman said. For the third quarter, Zillow’s revenue rose 7% to $724 million, short of its own forecast of $745 million to $760 million, as a sharp rise in mortgage rates slowed home sales. The company posted a $158 million net loss for the quarter, mostly from agreeing to settle a shareholder lawsuit over Zillow Offers, its defunct home-flipping business.
articles.author: Todd Bishop

articles.title: Canadian professor warns massive new data center would release ‘23 Hiroshima-sized atomic bombs worth of energy’ every day
articles.content: Celebrity investor Kevin O’Leary’s Wonder Valley data center plans are under scrutiny The Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation (SLCN) has filed for a judicial review over the project, which is planned to be the world’s largest data center A physicist hired by the SLCN has declared the data center will release significant heat waste A physicist acting on behalf of the Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation (SLCN) has claimed that the O’Leary Digital Wonder Valley data center would release “23 atomic bombs of energy” while adding that the declaration is “a first-order estimate intended to convey scale.” The report by Utah State University physicist Robert Davies, working on behalf of the SLCN, whose lawyer, also adds that current regulations for developing land are not suited to projects of the data center’s scale. O’Leary Digital Wonder Valley, plans for which were first unveiled in 2024, was conceived to be the largest on the planet when completed, and has a $70 billion budget for the 64 square kilometer (almost 15815 acres) development. Its planned location is in the SLCN’s traditional territory in Alberta, Canada. First-order estimate The planned scale of the data center, earmarked for a location 130 km southwest of the SLCN’s reserve, is the main point of contention, and the basis for Professor Robert Davies, of the Utah State University. But his claim over the “23 atomic bombs of energy” demands some clarification. "Now of course, that’s not explosions, but that’s just trying to get a sense of how much energy we’re talking about,” said Davies in the assessment. “The effect will almost certainly be large, if not extreme.” He also notes that “every quantitative figure … should be treated as a first-order estimate intended to convey scale, to be confirmed against the developer's own filings.” Davies also highlights that the project could be “the largest single-site heat source on the entire planet.” The assessment, which was prepared for SLCN’s case, emphasizes that it is “not a comprehensive environmental review, a formal expert report, or a legal opinion.” Robust regulatory process While Davies’ contribution to the SLCN’s judicial review filing relies on further information from O’Leary Digital, it paints a worrying picture, not least into the effects of the heat waste on the surrounding wildlife. "I can't imagine allowing it to go forward without those full assessments,” Davies said, while also criticizing the use of traditional environmental legislation and guidelines for giant data center projects. “When people talk about environmental regulations that these projects have to adhere to, those regulations were not created with anything of this scale in mind.” Naturally, O’Leary Digital has responded to the filing. CEO Paul Palandjian wrote in an email “We also respect the robust and stringent regulatory process we must follow in advancing Wonder Valley… we’re having productive dialogue with Indigenous communities through consultation and engagement, and we remain committed to that work."
articles.author: Christian Cawley
articles.fingerprint: atomic bombs canadian center data day energy every hiroshima massive professor release sized warns worth would
