articles.title: I spent a morning with Meta VR Glasses and wish I never had to take them off
articles.content: Experience counts for something, and nowhere is that more evident than on the Meta VR Glasses I finally wore this morning. These lightweight, intuitive, and engrossing VR glasses shed the weight and overdesigned fussiness of previous VR and mixed reality headsets to deliver a subtle, smart, eminently comfortable and fun wearable experience that is equally at home entertaining you with wild VR movies or expansive, productivity-enhancing virtual desktops. Granted, my walkthrough of the $1,299 VR Glasses that are expected to arrive next spring (April-early June) of next year was a breezy 45 minutes, but that was ample time to realize that Meta VR Glasses were truly built on all the lessons of not only Meta Quest VR, but also by watching competitors like Apple and even Samsung struggle to inspire consumers with stunning but also expensive or somewhat unwieldy mixed reality experiences. Lance Ulanoff / Future Lance Ulanoff / Future Lance Ulanoff / Future Lance Ulanoff / Future In my view, Meta's decision to move compute, storage, and battery out of the headset and into a 300g belt- or pocket-friendly puck pays design dividends. The wearable, which looks like a slightly oversized pair of sunglasses, is so comfortable that I barely felt them on my face, and after 45 minutes of continuous use, I didn't remove the 100-gram frames with a sense of relief. If anything, I was sad my all-too-brief interlude was over. Without needing to support CPUs, GPUs, NPUs, RAM, a heavy battery, or even SD storage, Meta could focus on basic aesthetic appeal. The Meta VR Glasses feel and look spare, but in a positive way. By design, they do not cut you off from the outside world (there will be an optional light shield), so there's no need to slap a pair of animated blinking eyes on the lenses. Granted, I had my doubts that the Meta VR Glasses would be all that immersive or inspiring, given what looked like essentially eye-sized lenses and no visible cameras, inside or out. That all turned out to be deceiving. Accurate tracking for an immersive experience (Image credit: Lance Ulanoff / Future) When I said Meta clearly learned from all that came before it, I wasn't kidding. The metaphors for setting up eye tracking were essentially the same as what I did for Apple Vision Pro (I didn't have to adjust pupillary distance, though you easily can) and, to an extent, Galaxy XR. You look at a circle of dots floating in space and, yes, use your fingers to pinch and select each one. There are, obviously, cameras that track your eyes, hands, and the outside world. I was impressed with the accuracy, which matched what I've experienced on Vision Pro. Equally, the first time I saw the floating menu, I was shocked at the visual quality (it's worth noting that Meta put in a pair of magnetic prescription inserts to match my eyes, and those inserts will probably add $150 to your final cost). For the record, Meta lists the Micro-OLED display resolution as 5K, and based on what I saw, I believe it. Disney+, a TV App, Avengers: Infinity War VR experience, and a dozen other app icons floated in space, with each one puffing up as I glanced at it. (Image credit: Lance Ulanoff / Future) Meta VR Glasses software doesn't try to reinvent the mixed reality wheel. I had no trouble opening apps, closing them, or even moving windows around. It does add one gesture that I appreciated: scroll. To scroll in any window, I made a gentle fist and then swiped my thumb across the side of my index finger to scroll left, right, up, and down. I was surprised at how quickly I picked this up; I think that has a lot to do with the accuracy of the eye and gesture tracking. My experiences were limited to a handful of apps, but each one was compelling in its own way. (Image credit: Meta) We started with an 8K VR Billie Eilish concert in which I was virtually seated front and center, close enough to take a selfie with the singer. The volume started a bit low for my tastes. Still, I was able to use the…

articles.title: X says its updated web app is way faster
articles.content: X is introducing a new version of its web app that it says is much faster than before, and it's now rolling out the updated app "one country at a time" for signed-in users. "Open a profile on X.com over a slow connection," principal engineer Yagiz Nizipli said in a blog post about the changes. "On the old web app, you'd stare at the X logo for more than 22 seconds before the first post appeared. On the new one, it shows up in 2.7." The post also goes into technical detail about how the updated app "replaces the three servers we used to run for people, search crawlers, and link previews with one." articles.title: Hands on: Siri Recaps & Live Rewind are controversial & unnecessary technologies
articles.content: After spending a day with Apple's Audio Intelligence features, they feel more like checked boxes than fully realized and useful features in spite of the clear privacy and boundaries present. Siri Recap and Live Rewind are odd features for Apple to offer When Apple first revealed Siri Recaps and Live Rewind during its September event, there was a lot of confusion and concern around the features . Now that they can be tested with the iOS 27.3 beta, I can say they are complicated to say the least. Siri Recaps will listen while you're in a specific location, like work, or during a certain period of time you've set. Users can have it active all day if they wish. Continue Reading on AppleInsider | Discuss on our Forums
articles.author: Wesley Hilliard <wes@appleinsider.com>

articles.title: Apple Releases Safari Technology Preview 256 With Bug Fixes and Performance Improvements
articles.content: Apple today released a new update for Safari Technology Preview , the experimental browser that was first introduced in March 2016. Apple designed ‌Safari Technology Preview‌ to allow users to test features that are planned for future release versions of the Safari browser. ‌Safari Technology Preview‌ 256 includes fixes and updates for Accessibility, Animations, CSS, Editing, Forms, HTML, JavaScript, Media, Networking, Rendering, SVG, Security, Web API, Web Extensions, Web Inspector, WebGL, and WebRTC. The current ‌Safari Technology Preview‌ release is compatible with machines running macOS Tahoe and macOS Golden Gate , the newest version of macOS. The ‌Safari Technology Preview‌ update is available through the Software Update mechanism in System Preferences or System Settings to anyone who has downloaded the browser from Apple's website. Complete release notes for the update are available on the Safari Technology Preview website . Apple's aim with ‌Safari Technology Preview‌ is to gather feedback from developers and users on its browser development process. ‌Safari Technology Preview‌ can run side-by-side with the existing Safari browser and while it is designed for developers, it does not require a developer account to download and use. API access is by request. ‌App Store‌ users may see offers for discounts or reasons to keep a subscription before canceling. articles.title: Tiny's new AI workstation is anything but — packing in 16 TB SSD array and 128 GB GPU memory, but with an eye-watering price tag to boot
articles.content: Tiny Corp's $30,000 tinybox Red Kimi pairs four Radeon AI Pro R9700 GPUs (128 GB GDDR6) with sixteen 1 TB NVMe SSDs A tinygrad driver lets the GPUs read the 238.4 GB/s SSD array directly to run Moonshot's 2.8-trillion-parameter Kimi K3 Tiny claims 40 tokens per second, but the math involves caching nearly all of each token's weights in VRAM There is nothing tiny about Tiny Corp's latest tinybox, the tinybox Red Kimi: It costs a mammoth $30,000 and pairs four AMD Radeon AI Pro R9700 graphics cards with sixteen 1 TB NVMe SSDs, all with one goal in mind: running Moonshot AI's 2.8-trillion-parameter Kimi K3 on a desk rather than in a data center. Each R9700 carries 32 GB of GDDR6 at 640 GB/s, giving the four cards 128 GB of GPU memory and 2,560 GB/s of aggregate bandwidth to go with a system built on Tiny Corp's G5 platform, with a 32-core AMD Epyc Genoa processor whose exact model the tinybox configurator doesn't name, and a modest 32 GB of DDR5 system memory in tow. Tiny Corp claims the machine can run Kimi K3 at 40 tokens per second, a figure nobody outside the company has tested yet. Sixteen drives, four GPUs and an AMD EPYC CPU rule the roost The storage in play is the unique selling point for Tiny Corp's behemoth: its 16 drives form a RAID array rated at 238.4 GB/s, and Tiny Corp says its tinygrad software now includes a driver that lets the AMD GPUs control the NVMe drives directly, rather than routing every read through the CPU. Sharing the system's topology on X , the company pitched the result as "frontier models at home at usable speeds for a good price." The rationale comes down to capacity. Moonshot's model card shows Kimi K3 ships with native MXFP4 weights, and Hyperstack measured the published checkpoint at roughly 1.56 TB. The four GPUs can hold about 8% of that, so the rest has to live somewhere, and Tiny Corp has picked considerably cheaper flash over DRAM. The concept isn't entirely new: Researchers from Nvidia and the University of Illinois presented GPU-initiated SSD access in the BaM system architecture at ASPLOS 2023, treating storage as another tier of accelerator memory. Tiny Corp's offering, however, is a working version on AMD workstation cards, inside a box you can actually order. The configurator's own code estimates the Red Kimi's installed weight at around 56 pounds, in a chassis 12 inches wide, 19.25 inches tall, and 18 inches deep. It also raises the noise rating from under 50 dB to under 60 dB for R9700 builds, warning that the cards' blower fans are "audible". Kimi K3 is a mixture-of-experts model that activates 16 of its 896 routed experts, plus two shared experts, for 104 billion active parameters per token. At MXFP4's effective 4.25 bits per weight, that means reading at least 55 GB of weights for every token generated. If every one of those bytes were read from the SSDs, the array would manage only about four tokens per second. Reaching 40 tokens per second means moving roughly 2.2 TB/s of weights, about 86% of the four GPUs' combined memory bandwidth, while the SSDs could contribute at most about 6 GB per token, or around 11% of what each one needs. In a nutshell, the claim only works if the GPUs' 128 GB already contains nearly everything each token touches, even though it fits less than a tenth of the model. That is achievable if expert selection is predictable enough to cache well, or if Tiny Corp is running a lower-precision quantization than Moonshot's native format, speculative decoding, or a mix of the three. Tiny Corp hasn't published the precision, context length, batch size, or method behind its number, and it would be prudent to treat it as a manufacturer claim at best. The aggregate bandwidth figure also assumes the workload is split evenly across four cards that communicate over PCIe. A pricey proposition that goes neck and neck with Apple's Mac Studio At $30,000, the Red Kimi is a lot of money for a desktop computer, but the alternatives for running a 2.8-trillion-parameter…

articles.title: Building AI factories at enterprise scale
articles.content: AI has become a juggernaut, driving technical strategy in the tech sector and outside of it. With the worldwide server market growing 30 percent in a single year to hit $122.6bn in the first quarter of 2025, IDC now feels safe recategorizing AI-driven investment "from cyclical to durable". The analyst company expects inference to account for over 70 percent of computing demand by next year, adding that it's growing fastest at the edge. Why enterprises are building their own All this investment in AI infrastructure might once have come mainly for hyperscalers, but that's changing quickly. Adoption is spreading quickly beyond public cloud service providers into enterprise environments, IDC adds. They're eager to run agentic AI in-house. There are plenty of reasons for companies to own their own AI infrastructure rather than offloading it to the cloud. One of these is data control, especially in regulated sectors such as finance, healthcare, manufacturing, and the public sector that have sovereign data requirements. Another revolves around the need for predictable costing from tokens delivered on tunable in-house systems. So what should companies look for in a supplier? Delivery speed will be a powerful driver for many who are under the gun to deliver AI initiatives for the business, especially during periods of constrained memory and CPU supply. Life cycle services will also come near the top of the list, for companies that need help managing everything from the power through to the reasoning LLM models and the workloads that use them. That need for expertise is unlikely to stop; companies will undergo changes in AI strategy as they get to grips with a still-evolving technology. From the desk to the datacenter ASUS expects this AI surge to continue in the datacenter, but elsewhere too, specifically in edge locations (especially industrial use cases) and at developers' desks, as the applications that will power the enterprise get made. It wants to be top of peoples' list for hardware and services at all these places along the AI continuum. At NVIDIA's GTC show in Berlin on Oct 21-22, it announced a full-stack AI offering that it's calling its Enterprise Agentic AI Solution . It's three-layer affair, featuring: ASUS AI Server and Infrastructure: Its selection of AI servers, including several new units. ASUS AI Software Stack: Its software for integrating and controlling AI workflows. ASUS AI HUB: A services operation that ties it all together. These bring together some existing assets that ASUS had for enterprise AI users, along with some new ones. The time is right for an end-to-end offering with new hardware because of the way the market is shifting, say ASUS execs. "ASUS servers help enterprises build high-performance agentic AI infrastructure capable of supporting both complex task execution and large-scale AI agent deployment, accelerating enterprise adoption of agentic AI," says Paul Ju, senior vice president and head of infrastructure solution BG at ASUS. While generative AI initially spiked demand, the advent of agentic AI has sent compute demand into overdrive. Ju explains that the focus is expanding from the GPU. "Historically, AI servers have been optimized primarily around GPU compute. But as enterprise AI shifts toward agentic AI, workloads increasingly revolve around a continuous ‘agent loop’ that is heavily CPU-dependent," he says. That loop takes in task planning, code execution, external tool invocation, and reflection or correction work. The CPU's increased role in this execution work is creating bottlenecks in conventional AI servers, he adds. The first such sticking point is single-thread performance, which leaves GPUs idling while they wait for CPUs to complete. The second lies in memory bandwidth. When this is managed on a per-core basis, it can slow things down when many agents run at once.
